| **Clawback** | Recovering previously paid comp after a restatement, breach, or misconduct. |
| **Garden leave** | Paid notice period during which a departing employee is not permitted to work. |
| **Non-compete / non-solicit** | Contractual restrictions on joining competitors or poaching colleagues; enforceability varies. |
| **Carry / LTIP** | Long-term incentive plan, often tied to firm value or fund profits. |
| **Phantom equity** | A contractual right to a share of value without actual ownership. |
| **RFP** | Request for Proposal; used in vendor and partnership selection. |
| **TCA** | Transaction Cost Analysis; measuring execution quality vs benchmarks. |
| **Exchange certification** | Formal testing required by an exchange before a member can connect or deploy algorithms. |
| **Corporate action** | Events like splits, dividends, mergers, and symbol changes that affect positions and data. |
| **Reconciliation break** | A mismatch between internal records and broker/exchange/custodian records. |
| **Settlement / clearing** | The post-trade process of transferring securities and cash, and the counterparty guarantee in between. |
| **Prime broker** | A bank that provides financing, custody, and settlement services to a trading firm. |
| **Counterparty risk** | The risk that a trading partner, broker, or exchange defaults. |
| **Liquidity risk** | The risk of being unable to fund or exit positions at a reasonable price. |
| **Surveillance** | Monitoring for market abuse, manipulation, and policy violations. |
| **Best execution** | The obligation (where applicable) to obtain the best possible result for client orders. |
| **MiFID II / EMIR / SEC / CFTC** | Major regulatory regimes/frameworks; obligations vary by jurisdiction and entity. |
| **SR 11-7** | US Federal Reserve guidance on model risk management; widely used as a reference standard. |

chapters.title: Appendix C — Promotion packet template
chapters.markdown:
## Appendix C — Promotion packet template

**Section 1 — Header**

```
Candidate:            [Name]
Current band/title:   [L2 · Quant Researcher]
Proposed band/title:  [L3 · Senior Quant Researcher]
Track:                [Research]
Manager:              [Name]
Sponsor:              [Name, band]
Cycle:                [2026 H2]
```

**Section 2 — Scope change (the core test)**

> What will this person own after promotion that they do not own today? Be specific about **decisions**, **horizon**, and **people**.

*Example:* "Owns the short-horizon equity alpha family (4 signals, ~X% of desk risk budget) end-to-end, including the G2/G3 gates, capacity estimates, and the research agenda for one L1 analyst. Currently owns one signal and no research agenda."

**Section 3 — Evidence (already operating at the next band)**

| Evidence type | Specific example | Impact (quantified) | Date |
|---|---|---|---|
| Strategy/system delivered | Signal X moved to production; net Sharpe Y over 14 months | +Z bps of firm P&L; capacity N units | Q1–Q4 2026 |
| Scope beyond own work | Led the leakage audit standard adopted by 3 pods | Reduced failed G2 gates by 40% | Q2 2026 |
| Mentorship | Mentored 2 L1s; one promoted | Both now own modules independently | 2025–2026 |
| Cross-functional influence | Drove data-quality SLA with CDO team | Data incidents down 30% | Q3 2026 |
| External signal | Presented at [conference]; paper under review | Firm brand; recruiting pipeline | 2026 |

**Section 4 — Peer and stakeholder feedback**

| Reviewer | Relationship | Would you trust them at L3? (Y/N) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Name] | Desk head | Y | "Owned the strategy through the March drawdown without changing the thesis." |
| [Name] | Risk | Y | "Escalated a limit issue early; proposed a fix." |
| [Name] | Peer QR | Y | "Review comments changed how I test for leakage." |

**Section 5 — Development areas (honest)**

- What is the biggest gap to the next band? (e.g., "has not yet led a cross-team project")
- What is the plan to close it? (specific, dated)
- What risk does promotion create? (e.g., "may over-index on research and neglect mentoring")

**Section 6 — Sponsor statement**

> "I have seen [Name] operate at L3 scope for [period] in [specific situations]. I would trust them to [specific next-band decision] without review. My main reservation is [X], which I believe is manageable because [Y]."

**Section 7 — Committee decision**

```
Decision:         [Promote / Defer / Not yet]
Effective date:   [Date]
New comp band:    [Index / range]
Conditions:       [e.g., complete manager training; 6-month check-in]
Rationale:        [2–3 sentences]
Committee chair:  [Name]
```

chapters.title: Appendix D — 90-day onboarding plans
chapters.markdown:
## Appendix D — 90-day onboarding plans

**Universal 30/60/90 structure**

| Phase | Goal | Deliverables | Check-in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Days 1–30** | Learn the firm, the data, the systems, and the people | Map of systems and stakeholders; one small shipped fix; 1:1s with 10+ people | Week 2 and week 4 with manager |
| **Days 31–60** | Own a real piece of work with support | First independent deliverable; documented assumptions; one design review | Week 6 |
| **Days 61–90** | Operate at band with minimal supervision | Owned outcome; written 90-day retrospective; development plan for next 6 months | Week 12 |

**Track-specific first 90 days**

| Track | Days 1–30 | Days 31–60 | Days 61–90 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Research** | Reproduce a known signal; learn the backtester and cost model; read 5 internal research memos | Own a small research question end-to-end; present at research review | Deliver a G1/G2-ready memo; identify one dead idea to kill |
| **Trading** | Shadow a trader; learn order types, limits, and kill switches; run a simulated book | Run a small live book under supervision; complete an incident drill | Own the book within limits; write a strategy note |
| **Technology** | Map the tick-to-trade path; ship a small fix; join on-call shadow | Own a module; complete a design review; handle one incident | Improve an SLO metric; document a runbook |
| **Data/ML** | Map data sources and lineage; fix one pipeline bug; learn the feature store | Own a dataset or pipeline; add tests and monitoring | Deliver a data quality improvement with measurable impact |
| **Risk** | Learn every limit and where it is enforced; shadow daily reporting | Own a risk domain; run a stress test; challenge one assumption | Present a risk finding to the Risk Committee |
| **Compliance/Legal** | Build the obligations register; review filings; meet key exchanges | Own a compliance process; draft a policy or contract | Complete a mock exam or regulatory review |
| **Finance/Treasury** | Trace a trade from execution to GL; learn the close; meet bankers | Own a reconciliation or treasury process | Improve close time or funding cost measurably |
| **Operations** | Learn the trade lifecycle; shadow connectivity and settlements | Own a process; write a runbook; handle a break | Lead an incident drill; automate one manual step |
| **Product/Business** | Interview 10 internal users; map the platform and partners | Own a product area or deal pipeline | Ship a small improvement or close a deal milestone |

**Onboarding anti-patterns:** no named buddy; no first-week deliverable; "read the wiki" as the plan; no introduction to the desks; no clear 90-day success criteria; leaving the new hire to figure out the informal org alone.

chapters.title: Appendix E — Interview question bank
chapters.markdown:
## Appendix E — Interview question bank

**Research**

1. Walk me through a signal you built. What was the economic mechanism, and how did you test it?
2. How do you detect data leakage in a backtest? Give a specific example.
3. Your signal has a Sharpe of 3 in backtest and 0.5 live. What do you check first?
4. How do you estimate capacity? What changes as capital grows?
5. When would you kill a strategy that is still profitable?
6. Explain a paper you disagree with. Why?
7. How would you test whether a machine-learning model is learning signal vs noise?
8. What is the difference between a statistically significant result and an economically meaningful one?

**Trading**

1. You have a position that is down 2% and your thesis is intact. What do you do?
2. How do you size a position when you are uncertain about your edge?
3. Explain adverse selection in market making. How do you manage it?
4. The market moves against you and your model says stay. How do you decide?
5. What is your worst trade, and what did you learn?
6. How do you know whether your P&L is skill or beta?
7. Walk me through your kill criteria for a strategy.
8. You see an unusual order pattern in the book. What do you do?

**Technology**

1. Design the path from market-data packet to order submission. Where does latency come from?
2. How do you make a lock-free queue correct? What are the memory-ordering pitfalls?
3. You have a p99 latency spike every 5 minutes. How do you debug it?
4. How do you design a system that must never lose an order?
5. What is your approach to testing a trading system that cannot be tested in production?
6. How do you handle a production incident at 3 a.m. with no obvious cause?
7. When would you choose FPGA over software? What are the trade-offs?
8. How do you prevent a bad deployment from taking down trading?

**Data / ML Engineering**

1. Design a tick-data store for 50 TB with point-in-time queries. What are the trade-offs?
2. How do you make a pipeline idempotent and backfillable?
3. A schema change silently breaks a downstream model. How do you prevent this?
4. How do you detect train/serve skew?
5. How do you govern access to licensed data?
6. What does "data quality" mean for tick data vs reference data?
7. How do you decide between batch and streaming?
8. How do you measure the cost of a data platform?

**Risk / Model Validation**

1. Critique a VaR model that assumes normal returns. What breaks?
2. How would you design limits for a new market-making strategy?
3. A senior trader wants a limit increase during a drawdown. What do you do?
4. How do you validate a machine-learning alpha model?
5. What is the difference between model risk and market risk?
6. How do you stress test a portfolio with options and illiquid positions?
7. What would make you escalate to the board?
8. How do you know your validation is independent enough?

**Compliance / Legal**

1. A new product launches in two weeks in a new jurisdiction. What do you check?
2. How do you detect spoofing or layering in order data?
3. What are the reporting obligations for the instruments we trade?
4. A trader's personal account trades the same instrument. What is the issue?
5. How do you handle a regulator request for historical order data?
6. When should compliance say "no" vs "here's how"?
7. What data-licensing restrictions apply to alternative data?
8. How do you keep the firm current on regulatory change?

**Finance / Treasury**

1. Trace a trade from execution to the general ledger. Where can it break?
2. How do you build a 13-week cash forecast for a trading firm?
3. What is the cost of holding collateral, and how do you optimize it?
4. How do you attribute P&L to strategy vs market moves?
5. What controls prevent a rogue payment?
6. How do you decide whether to repatriate or reinvest foreign profits?
7. What is the tax risk in a multi-entity trading structure?
8. How do you present risk-adjusted returns to the board?

**Operations**

1. Walk me through the trade lifecycle from order to settlement.
2. An exchange changes its API the day before expiry. What do you do?
3. How do you resolve a reconciliation break that is 3 days old?
4. Design the incident response for a connectivity outage at the open.
5. What is the difference between clearing and settlement?
6. How do you manage corporate actions across 20 venues?
7. What single-person dependencies exist in your current process?
8. How do you measure operational risk?

**Product / Business**

1. How do you decide what to build for a desk that says "everything is urgent"?
2. Tell me about a product that failed. Why?
3. How do you negotiate an exchange fee schedule?
4. What makes an internal platform adopted vs ignored?
5. How do you measure the ROI of a partnership?
6. A partner misses a deadline that affects trading. What do you do?
7. How do you prioritize between two desks with conflicting needs?
8. What would you stop doing in your first 90 days?

chapters.title: Appendix G — Further reading
chapters.markdown:
## Appendix G — Further reading

**Market microstructure and trading**

- Larry Harris, *Trading and Exchanges: Market Microstructure for Practitioners* — the definitive practitioner reference.
- Maureen O'Hara, *Market Microstructure Theory* — the academic foundation.
- Irene Aldridge, *High-Frequency Trading: A Practical Guide to Algorithmic Strategies and Trading Systems* — applied HFT.
- Robert Carver, *Systematic Trading* and *Leveraged Trading* — portfolio construction and realistic backtesting for systematic traders.
- Ernest Chan, *Algorithmic Trading: Winning Strategies and Their Rationale* — accessible strategy design with code.

**Research methodology and overfitting**

- Marcos López de Prado, *Advances in Financial Machine Learning* — data structures, labeling, backtest pitfalls.
- Marcos López de Prado, *Machine Learning for Asset Managers* — compact treatment of ML in portfolio construction.
- Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado, Zhu, "The Probability of Backtest Overfitting" — the deflated Sharpe framework.
- Bailey & López de Prado, "The Deflated Sharpe Ratio" — correcting for selection bias.
- Grinold & Kahn, *Active Portfolio Management* — the canonical text on alpha, risk, and portfolio construction.
- David Aronson, *Evidence-Based Technical Analysis* — statistical rigor for trading rules.

**Risk and governance**

- John Hull, *Risk Management and Financial Institutions* — comprehensive risk framework.
- Philippe Jorion, *Value at Risk* — VaR/ES foundations and limitations.
- Federal Reserve SR 11-7, *Guidance on Model Risk Management* — the reference standard for model risk.
- Basel Committee papers on stress testing and risk appetite — framework language regulators expect.
- Nassim Taleb, *Antifragile* and *The Black Swan* — tail-risk intuition (read critically).

**Engineering and reliability**

- Martin Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* — data systems foundations.
- Google SRE team, *Site Reliability Engineering* and *The Site Reliability Workbook* — SLOs, error budgets, incident management.
- Will Larson, *Staff Engineer* — the IC leadership path.
- Will Larson, *An Elegant Puzzle* — engineering org design and management.
- Camille Fournier, *The Manager's Path* — the transition from IC to manager.
- Andy Grove, *High Output Management* — the classic on managerial leverage.

**Firm strategy and history**

- Gregory Zuckerman, *The Man Who Solved the Market* — Renaissance Technologies and the culture of quant research.
- Sebastian Mallaby, *More Money Than God* — hedge fund history and strategy evolution.
- Scott Patterson, *Dark Pools* — the rise of electronic trading and HFT.
- Michael Lewis, *Flash Boys* — readable but polemical; read alongside Harris and Patterson.

**Execution and market making theory**

- Almgren & Chriss, "Optimal Execution of Portfolio Transactions" — the foundational execution model.
- Avellaneda & Stoikov, "High-Frequency Trading in a Limit Order Book" — market-making model.
- Robert Almgren, "Execution Risk" — practical treatment of execution uncertainty.

**Regulatory references (jurisdiction-specific; verify current versions)**

- SEC Rule 15c3-5 (Market Access Rule) — pre-trade risk controls for US broker-dealers.
- MiFID II / MiFIR, including RTS 6 on algorithmic trading — EU algorithmic controls and reporting.
- EMIR — EU derivatives clearing and reporting.
- CFTC Part 43/45 — US swaps reporting (where applicable).
- Local exchange rulebooks — connectivity, certification, and market-conduct rules.

**Companion resource in this workspace**

- `youtube-quant-hft-resources.md` — a curated list of ~95 quant/HFT talks, lectures, and channels for ongoing learning.

chapters.title: Appendix H — Original source text (preserved verbatim)
chapters.markdown:
## Appendix H — Original source text (preserved verbatim)

> This appendix reproduces the two sections supplied at the start of the project, exactly as written, so the source of the framework is never lost. Part II expands Section 1; Part III (§11–§14) and Part IV expand Section 2.

### H.1 Core Domains & Job Titles

**Research & Strategy**

- **Quantitative Researcher (QR) / Alpha Researcher:** Builds statistical, econometric, and machine learning models to predict short-term price moves and market microstructure signals.
- **Execution / Microstructure Researcher:** Studies order-book dynamics, queue position, slippage, and optimal order routing.
- **Data Quant / Alternative Data Researcher:** Sources, cleans, and models tick data, order books, news, and alternative datasets.

**Trading & Portfolio Management**

- **Quantitative Trader (QT):** Runs live strategies, monitors risk and P&L, tunes parameters, and manages intraday/short-horizon exposures.
- **Execution Trader:** Focuses on low-impact order execution, liquidity provision, and market making across exchanges.
- **Portfolio Manager (PM) / Quant PM:** Owns P&L for a book or strategy pod, allocates capital and risk limits, and leads researchers/traders.

**Software, Low-Latency & Hardware Engineering**

- **Quantitative Developer (QD):** Turns research models and trading logic into fast, reliable production code (heavily C++, Rust, or Python).
- **Low-Latency / HFT Systems Engineer:** Optimizes kernel bypass, networking, lock-free concurrency, and tick-to-trade latency.
- **FPGA / Hardware Engineer:** Designs custom hardware logic (Verilog/VHDL/FPGA) for ultra-low-latency market data decoding and order execution.
- **Core / Infrastructure / SRE / DevOps Engineer:** Builds distributed compute clusters, simulation/backtesting pipelines, telemetry, and production reliability.

**Data, Risk & Control**

- **Data Engineer / Machine Learning Engineer:** Builds petabyte-scale historical tick storage, feature pipelines, and ML training infrastructure.
- **Quantitative Risk Manager / Risk Engineer:** Monitors real-time exposure, stress tests tail risk, enforces margin/position limits, and validates models.
- **Model Validation Quant:** Independently tests pricing, risk, and statistical assumptions for accuracy and robustness.

**Operations & Corporate Functions**

- **Trading Operations / Market Ops:** Handles exchange connectivity, corporate actions, reconciliations, and live incident response.
- **Compliance, Legal & Finance:** Manages regulatory reporting, exchange rules, treasury, and firm accounting.

### H.2 Typical Ranks & Career Progression

Exact titles vary by firm, but most HFT and quant shops follow a flat-to-tiered meritocratic ladder tied closely to P&L or technical impact:

1. **Intern / Summer Analyst:** Short-term research, trading simulation, or coding projects; primary pipeline for full-time offers.
2. **Junior / Associate / Analyst (Entry-Level, ~0–2 yrs):** Executes defined research tasks, builds basic tools, or assists on live trading desks under supervision.
3. **Mid-Level Quant / Trader / Developer (~2–5 yrs):** Independently owns signals, trading books, or core low-latency systems.
4. **Senior Quant / Senior Trader / Senior Engineer (~5+ yrs):** Leads complex strategies or mission-critical infrastructure and mentors junior staff.
5. **Vice President (VP) / Director / Principal:** Used more often at banks and larger multi-strat funds; denotes high technical or desk authority.
6. **Portfolio Manager (PM) / Head of Desk:** Runs a standalone profit center or team with explicit capital and risk budgets.
7. **Managing Director (MD) / Partner / C-Suite (CEO, CTO, CRO, Head of Quant):** Shapes firm-wide strategy, capital allocation, risk governance, and leadership.

**Mapping to this document:** H.1 is expanded in Part II (with scope notes, interfaces, and bands); H.2 is preserved and mapped to the unified ladder in §11 ("The original seven-rank ladder") and expanded into full journeys in Part IV.

chapters.title: Closing note
chapters.markdown:
## Closing note

This framework is a **default, not a dogma**. The bands, gates, and committees exist to make the implicit explicit — so that a firm can grow without losing the things that made it good: small teams, fast decisions, real ownership, and an honest relationship with risk.

Three questions to ask every year:

1. **Is our structure still following our edge?** If the edge moved, the org should move.
2. **Do our levels still mean something?** If a band no longer predicts scope, fix the calibration.
3. **Would a strong person join us and know how to grow here?** If not, the career framework is not finished.

*Version 1.0 · November 2026 · Maintained by the CEO office. Review annually, or whenever the firm crosses a scaling threshold.*

levels.title: Intern / Summer Analyst
levels.autonomy: supervised; you ask before changing direction.
levels.mission: prove you can learn fast, work with data, and communicate clearly.
levels.scope: one well-defined project with a named supervisor and a written brief.
levels.deliverables: a working analysis, notebook, or tool; a short presentation; a written handoff.
levels.promotion: an offer to return at L1 — not because the project succeeded, but because the reasoning and collaboration were sound.
levels.titles: Summer Analyst, Research Intern, Trading Intern, Software Engineering Intern.
levels.good: the work is reproducible, the conclusion is honest, and the intern can explain why the method was chosen.

levels.title: Analyst / Associate
levels.autonomy: guided; the supervisor sets the what, you own the how within agreed bounds.
levels.mission: execute defined work reliably and start forming judgment.
levels.scope: a component of a larger project — a data pipeline, a backtest module, a risk report, a reconciliation.
levels.deliverables: clean code/analysis, documented assumptions, on-time delivery, clear status updates.
levels.decisions: none over capital or production; may propose improvements.
levels.promotion: consistent independent delivery, correct use of statistical/engineering fundamentals, and evidence of why not just what.
levels.titles: Analyst, Associate, Junior Quant, Junior Trader, Graduate Engineer.

levels.title: Quant / Trader / Engineer
levels.owns: A signal, module, or book slice
levels.autonomy: independent on day-to-day decisions; escalates design changes and limit exceptions.
levels.mission: own a meaningful piece of the machine end-to-end.
levels.scope: one signal, one execution module, one risk model, one platform service, or a slice of a book.
levels.deliverables: a production-quality signal/system with tests, monitoring, documentation; a measurable contribution to P&L, latency, uptime, or risk coverage.
levels.decisions: may deploy within sandbox/limits; may approve small technical changes; cannot change firm risk limits.
levels.promotion: owns outcomes, not tasks; handles ambiguity; their work is used by others without rework.
levels.titles: Quant Researcher, Quant Trader, Quant Developer, Software Engineer, Data Engineer, Risk Analyst.

levels.title: Senior QR / QT / QD
levels.owns: A strategy, system, or desk function
levels.autonomy: sets own priorities within the mandate; makes technical calls; represents the firm in their domain.
levels.people: leads projects and 1–3 juniors; not yet a people manager.
levels.mission: own a strategy, system, or function that materially moves the firm's numbers.
levels.scope: a full strategy from hypothesis to production, a critical platform, or a desk function (execution, risk coverage, data platform).
levels.deliverables: strategy P&L or platform SLOs; a documented research/engineering agenda; mentorship of L1–L2; cross-team design reviews.
levels.decisions: can approve production changes in their domain; can spend within a small budget; can veto unsafe technical choices (with escalation path).
levels.promotion: repeatable success across more than one project; influence beyond their own work; ability to say "no" with evidence.
levels.titles: Senior Quant Researcher, Senior Trader, Senior Software Engineer, Senior Data Engineer, Senior Risk Analyst.

levels.title: Staff / Principal / Desk Lead
levels.autonomy: sets direction for the area; negotiates priorities with L5+; owns technical or trading standards.
levels.people: leads 3–10 ICs (directly or matrixed); coaches L3s.
levels.mission: multiply other people's output — through architecture, strategy, or desk leadership.
levels.scope: a platform, a multi-strategy cluster, a research program, or a desk of 2–5 pods.
levels.deliverables: platform roadmap or strategy cluster P&L; standards, tooling, and reviews that raise the whole team; a pipeline of L2–L3 talent.
levels.decisions: allocates technical resources within the area; approves designs; may own a small P&L or cost center.
levels.promotion: the area runs better because you exist; you are the person others consult before a major decision; you have built something that outlives your direct involvement.
levels.titles: Staff Quant Researcher, Principal Engineer, Staff Data Engineer, Desk Lead, Research Lead.

levels.title: Manager / Head of Desk
levels.autonomy: allocates capital within risk limits; hires/fires (with calibration); sets desk strategy.
levels.people: manages ICs and L4 leads; builds the bench.
levels.mission: own a P&L and the team that produces it.
levels.scope: a desk (2–5 pods) or a function with a clear mandate and budget.
levels.deliverables: risk-adjusted P&L; team development; capacity and cost management; strategy pipeline.
levels.decisions: capital allocation within limits, position limits within CRO-approved bands, compensation recommendations, vendor spend within budget.
levels.promotion: sustained P&L through different regimes; a team that performs without you in the room; clean risk and compliance record; succession plan in place.
levels.titles: Head of Desk, Trading Manager, Research Manager, Engineering Manager, Risk Manager.

levels.title: Director / Head of Function
levels.autonomy: sets function strategy; owns the budget; represents the function at the executive table.
levels.mission: own a function's strategy and its interface with the rest of the firm.
levels.scope: Research, Technology, Risk, Data, Finance, Operations, Compliance, or Product — multiple teams and managers.
levels.deliverables: function roadmap; talent strategy; cross-functional agreements (SLAs, risk appetite, tech standards); regulatory standing.
levels.decisions: function budget, org design, vendor selection, prioritization; co-owns firm-level decisions with C-suite.
levels.promotion: the function is a competitive advantage, not a support center; peers trust the function's judgment; you can run the firm's agenda in your domain.
levels.titles: Head of Research, Head of Technology, Head of Risk, Head of Data, Head of Finance, Head of Operations, Head of Compliance, Director.

levels.title: VP / SVP / Deputy C-Suite
levels.autonomy: sets policy within the C-suite's mandate; acts for the C-suite officer when delegated.
levels.people: leads L6 managers; shapes the leadership pipeline.
levels.mission: own a firm-wide domain or a major sub-function at scale.
levels.scope: a domain that spans teams and geographies — e.g., Global Execution, Research Platform, Risk Analytics, Treasury, Legal.
levels.deliverables: firm-wide standards, multi-year roadmap, regulatory relationships, major change programs.
levels.decisions: delegated authority from a C-suite officer; represents the firm externally in the domain.
levels.promotion: trusted to run the domain without supervision; external recognition; succession-ready for L8.
levels.titles: SVP Engineering, VP Risk, Deputy CTO, Global Head of Execution, Head of Legal.

levels.title: C-Suite
levels.autonomy: full functional authority; co-owns firm strategy with the CEO and peers.
levels.people: leads the function's leadership team; develops L7 successors.
levels.mission: own a firm-wide function and its contribution to firm strategy.
levels.scope: Technology, Risk, Finance, Operations, Compliance/Legal, Data, Research, Trading, or Business — depending on the firm's structure.
levels.deliverables: functional strategy, capital/risk/tech agenda, regulatory relationships, leadership bench, board reporting.
levels.decisions: function budget and org; firm-level policies in the domain; veto rights where the domain requires independence (CRO, CCO).
levels.promotion: the board and CEO trust the function's judgment; the function is audit-clean and strategy-aligned; a credible successor exists.
levels.titles: CTO, CRO, CFO, COO, CCO, General Counsel, CDO, Chief Scientist, Head of Strategies/Chief Trading Officer.

levels.title: CEO
levels.people: leads the C-suite; builds the next CEO.
levels.mission: set the firm's strategy, allocate capital across businesses, and own the final trade-off between risk and return.
levels.scope: the entire firm — strategy, capital, people, culture, regulatory standing, board and investor relationships.
levels.deliverables: firm strategy and capital plan; executive team; risk appetite; external relationships; succession.
levels.decisions: final call on capital allocation, M&A, new businesses, C-suite appointments (with board), and firm-wide risk appetite.

tracks.title: Research track (QR / ML / microstructure / alt-data / portfolio optimization)
tracks.entry_points: PhD or Master's in statistics, ML, mathematics, physics, CS, economics; exceptional undergraduates with research evidence; internships converted from L0. Lateral hires from other funds, banks, or big-tech research.

ladder.title: Senior QR
ladder.kpis: Net Sharpe of family, research-to-prod conversion

ladder.title: Head of Research
ladder.scope: All research pods, budget, hiring bar

ladder.title: Chief Scientist / SVP Research
ladder.scope: External reputation, PhD pipeline, long-horizon bets

tracks.branches: alpha/statistical arbitrage, ML/deep learning, market microstructure, alternative data, portfolio optimization, execution research.
tracks.lateral: QR → QT (with trading mentorship), QR → model validation (risk), QR → data science/product, QR → research management.
tracks.failure_modes: overfitting to backtests; never shipping; ignoring transaction costs; single-regime dependence; poor documentation; treating research review as a formality; refusing to kill a dead idea.
tracks.promotion_evidence: two or more signals in production, at least one with 12+ months live attribution; documented OOS protocol; mentorship of an L1; a research review presentation that survived adversarial questioning.

narrative.text: learn the craft. Reproduce papers, build clean datasets, run honest backtests. The goal is not a great idea; it is not fooling yourself. Master the data, the backtester, and the cost model.
own one signal from hypothesis to production. Learn why most ideas die: costs, capacity, regime dependence, data leakage. Ship something small and real.
own a family of signals. Develop taste for which ideas are worth pursuing. Mentor juniors. Present at research review and defend your assumptions.
set methodology. Build the research platform's standards, the replication protocol, the kill criteria. Your impact is now through other researchers.
lead the function. Balance long-horizon research with near-term P&L; protect research independence from desk pressure; own the hiring bar.

tracks.title: Trading track (QT / execution / market making / PM)
tracks.entry_points: quantitative degrees, internships, prop trading, poker/competitive games, military/ops discipline, lateral hires from other desks. Trading is the most apprenticeship-heavy track; simulation and live mentorship matter more than credentials.

ladder.title: Junior Trader
ladder.mission: Run a small book under supervision

ladder.title: Quant Trader
ladder.kpis: Net P&L, Sharpe, drawdown, fill quality

ladder.title: Senior Trader
ladder.mission: Own a strategy family / desk function

ladder.title: Head of Trading / Strategies
ladder.kpis: Firm trading P&L, capacity, market entry

tracks.branches: market making, execution, systematic directional, options/volatility, crypto, cross-asset.
tracks.lateral: QT → QR (research depth), QT → product/BD (market structure expertise), QT → risk (desk experience is valuable), QT → management.
tracks.failure_modes: overriding risk limits; increasing size to recover losses; hiding drawdowns; mistaking a bull regime for skill; poor handoffs; burning out on night sessions.
tracks.promotion_evidence: 12–24 months of positive risk-adjusted P&L through at least one drawdown; zero limit breaches; documented strategy logic; mentorship of an L1; a clear capacity estimate.

narrative.text: learn to not lose money. Risk limits are training wheels, not insults. Master the mechanics: order types, queue, slippage, settlement, corporate actions.
own a book. Learn position sizing, correlation, and the difference between edge and luck. Survive your first drawdown without changing strategy mid-flight.
own a strategy family. Adapt across regimes. Mentor juniors. Learn to communicate P&L attribution clearly to risk and management.
lead a desk. Allocate capital, build a strategy pipeline, manage a team of strong personalities. Your job is now capital allocation and talent, not just trading.
run trading as a business. Decide which markets to enter/exit, how much capital each desk gets, and how the firm's risk appetite evolves.

tracks.title: Technology track (QD / low-latency / FPGA / infra / SRE / security)
tracks.entry_points: CS/EE degrees, systems programming, competitive programming, kernel/networking hobbies, FPGA projects, lateral hires from HFT, big tech, or exchanges.
tracks.branches: low-latency/HFT, FPGA/hardware, infrastructure/SRE, security, data platform, application/platform engineering, build/release.
tracks.lateral: tech → research engineering, tech → product, tech → ops (connectivity), tech → CTO track.
tracks.failure_modes: over-engineering; hero-driven operations; ignoring p99/jitter; security debt; refusing to document; optimizing for elegance over trading outcomes.
tracks.promotion_evidence: owned a critical subsystem through at least one major incident; measurable SLO improvement; design review leadership; mentorship; cross-team adoption of a tool or standard.

narrative.text: learn to write code that other people can trust. Tests, reviews, observability, on-call. Understand the trading domain enough to ask better questions.
own a production module. Feel the pain of p99 latency and 3 a.m. incidents. Learn to debug under pressure.
own a critical subsystem. Design for failure. Mentor. Learn to say "no" to features that add latency or operational risk.
set architecture. Choose build vs buy, co-location strategy, language/runtime, hardware roadmap. Your leverage is now standards and platform.
lead engineering. Balance delivery speed with reliability and security. Build a bench of L4s.

tracks.title: Data & ML Engineering track
tracks.entry_points: CS/statistics/engineering degrees; data platform engineering at scale-ups; ML infrastructure; database internals; lateral hires from big tech, exchanges, or other funds. The distinguishing test is not "can you use Spark" but "can you make 50 TB of tick data queryable, correct, and cheap at 3 a.m. before the open."

ladder.title: Data Engineer / MLE
ladder.scope: Tick store, feature store, or model service
ladder.kpis: SLA adherence, cost per TB, model latency

ladder.title: Senior DE / Senior MLE
ladder.mission: Own the data platform or ML platform

ladder.title: Head of Data / Head of ML

tracks.branches: market data engineering, tick/order-book storage, feature platforms, MLOps/model serving, data governance & lineage, alternative-data ingestion.
tracks.lateral: data → research engineering; data → quant research (strong candidates with statistics); data → technology platform; data → risk data/regulatory reporting.
tracks.failure_modes: pipelines without tests; silent schema drift; "the data is always right" assumptions; building a platform nobody uses; hoarding data access instead of governing it; confusing tool adoption with data quality.
tracks.promotion_evidence: platform or domain owned through at least one production data incident; measurable freshness/quality improvement; lineage and documentation adopted by others; a research team that ships faster because of your work.

narrative.text: learn that data work is 80% correctness and 20% cleverness. Build pipelines with tests, idempotency, and backfills. Learn the difference between "the job ran" and "the data is right."

own a data domain — tick data, corporate actions, reference data, or a feature store. Feel the pain of a silent schema change and a stale partition on a live trading day. Build monitoring that catches it before the desk does.
own the platform. Design for cost, latency, and lineage. Learn that the hardest problem is not storage but semantics: two desks computing "volume" differently is a data incident waiting to happen.
set architecture. Lakehouse vs warehouse, batch vs streaming, build vs buy. Your job is to reduce the time from "researcher has an idea" to "researcher has clean data" from weeks to hours.
lead the function. Data governance, vendor licensing, regulatory data requests, and the political work of getting desks to adopt standards.

tracks.title: Risk & Model Validation track
tracks.entry_points: quantitative finance, statistics, physics, engineering; bank risk/validation teams; model risk management; trading desk lateral moves (with independence guardrails). Risk is a second line function: it must be credible to the desk without being captured by it.

ladder.title: Risk Analyst
ladder.gate: Independent coverage of a risk type

ladder.title: Risk Manager / Risk Engineer
ladder.kpis: Limit breaches caught pre-trade, stress quality
ladder.gate: Domain owned through a stress event

ladder.title: Senior Risk Manager
ladder.mission: Own the risk framework for a desk cluster

ladder.title: Risk Manager (people) / Head of Market Risk

tracks.branches: market risk, credit/counterparty risk, liquidity/treasury risk, model validation, operational risk, regulatory capital, climate/emerging risk (rare in prop).
tracks.lateral: risk → research (model-building skills transfer); risk → compliance (regulatory overlap); risk → trading (desk experience, but requires cooling-off and independence rules); risk → treasury.
tracks.failure_modes: becoming the desk's rubber stamp; reporting after the loss; VaR models that assume normality in a fat-tail market; validation that checks documentation instead of assumptions; escalation avoided to keep the peace.
tracks.promotion_evidence: caught a material risk before it materialized; designed limits adopted by multiple desks; led a stress event post-mortem; independent validation memo that changed a model or a limit.

narrative.text: learn the numbers and the plumbing. Reconcile exposures, run the daily limit report, understand every field. The goal is to be the person who notices the number is wrong before the desk does.
own a risk domain. Build pre-trade checks, stress scenarios, and limit logic. Learn to say "no" early and explain why in the desk's language — P&L, not policy.
own the framework for a cluster of desks. Design limits that bind without strangling. Run stress tests that the desk respects because they reflect real tail behavior.
set methodology and lead a team. Your credibility is your only currency; you cannot buy it with org charts. Build a validation function that finds real problems, not paperwork.
own the function. Advise the CEO on risk appetite, represent the firm to regulators, and hold the line when the desk is having its best month.

subtracks.title: Model Validation sub-track
rows: Validate one model family (pricing, risk, alpha)
Lead validation for a desk or model class; challenge assumptions
Own the validation standard, sampling, and revalidation cadence
Independent model risk function; report to CRO or board risk committee
Head of Model Risk / Deputy CRO
Firm-wide model risk governance, regulatory relationships

tracks.title: Compliance & Legal track
tracks.entry_points: law degrees (JD/LLB), compliance/regulatory backgrounds from banks or exchanges, surveillance analysts, paralegals, regulatory affairs. In a <100-person firm this is often one combined function; at scale it splits into Compliance (CCO) and Legal (GC).

ladder.title: Compliance Officer / Counsel
ladder.gate: Domain owned through a regulatory exam

ladder.title: Senior Compliance Officer / Senior Counsel
ladder.mission: Own the program for a business line

tracks.branches: trade surveillance, regulatory reporting (MiFID/EMIR/SEC/CFTC equivalents), exchange compliance, employment/comp legal, corporate/M&A, IP and data licensing, financial crime.
tracks.lateral: compliance → risk (overlapping control agendas); compliance → operations (regulatory ops); legal → corp dev; compliance → product (regulatory product design).
tracks.failure_modes: checkbox compliance; being surprised by a rule change; saying "no" without alternatives; treating the regulator as an adversary; legal advice that ignores commercial reality.
tracks.promotion_evidence: owned a regulatory exam or audit with no material findings; built a surveillance or reporting process adopted firm-wide; advised on a new market/product launch end-to-end.

narrative.text: learn the rulebook cold — exchange rules, market-abuse regulation, reporting deadlines, entity structures. Accuracy is the whole job.
own a domain: trade surveillance, regulatory reporting, licensing, or contracts. Build processes that survive an exam, not just a checklist.
own the program for a business line. Build relationships with regulators and exchanges. Learn to say "we can do this, but here's how" instead of "no."
set the program and lead a team. Your job is to make compliance a design input, not a post-hoc review.
own the function. Advise the board, manage regulatory strategy across jurisdictions, and protect the firm's license to operate.

tracks.title: Finance & Treasury track
tracks.entry_points: accounting (CPA/CA/ACCA), finance, economics; bank treasury/FP&A; audit; lateral hires from funds or brokers.
tracks.branches: accounting/control, treasury, tax, FP&A, capital planning, investor reporting, audit.
tracks.lateral: finance → risk (treasury/market risk overlap); finance → operations (settlements); finance → corp dev; finance → COO track.
tracks.failure_modes: books that close late; reconciliation debt; treasury surprises on margin calls; tax positions that don't survive scrutiny; finance that reports history but never informs decisions.
tracks.promotion_evidence: owned a clean audit; reduced close time or funding cost measurably; built a capital or treasury model used by the CEO.

narrative.text: learn the close, the chart of accounts, and how P&L actually flows from trades to the general ledger. Accuracy and speed.
own a domain — accounting, tax, treasury operations, or FP&A. Build controls that scale. Learn that a reconciliation break is a risk signal, not an annoyance.
own the finance calendar. Multi-entity, multi-currency, multi-broker. Manage audits and banking relationships.
set policy and lead. Capital allocation, transfer pricing, tax strategy, treasury risk. Your job is to fund the firm's edge at the lowest cost.
own the function. Board reporting, investor relations (with CEO), capital planning, and the trade-off between returning capital and reinvesting.

tracks.title: Operations track
tracks.entry_points: finance/operations/business degrees; exchange or broker operations; trade support; military logistics; lateral hires from funds or prime brokers. Operations is the firm's immune system: it is invisible when healthy and existential when not.
tracks.branches: trade support, market ops/connectivity, settlements & clearing, corporate actions, vendor management, business continuity, regulatory operations.
tracks.lateral: ops → risk (operational risk); ops → compliance (regulatory ops); ops → technology (production support); ops → trading (market mechanics expertise).
tracks.failure_modes: single-person processes; manual workarounds that become permanent; reconciliation debt; poor incident communication; treating ops as a cost center rather than a control.
tracks.promotion_evidence: owned a market event or exchange outage response; reduced break rate or MTTR measurably; automated a process that removed a key-person risk.

narrative.text: learn the trade lifecycle end to end — order, fill, allocation, settlement, reconciliation, corporate action. Be the person who catches the break.
own a domain. Exchange connectivity certifications, market-data entitlements, corporate actions, or clearing. Build runbooks. Automate the boring parts.
own the ops calendar. Coordinate across venues and time zones. Run incident response without drama.
set policy and lead. Vendor management, exchange relationships, cost control, and the operational side of new market entry.
own the function. Operational resilience, business continuity, multi-office coverage, and the COO agenda.

tracks.title: Product & Business track
tracks.entry_points: product management, consulting, banking/BD, exchange or vendor roles, internal transfers from trading or technology. This track is optional below ~150 people; it becomes essential when the firm builds internal platforms or external partnerships.

ladder.title: Product Analyst / BD Analyst
ladder.scope: One product area or deal pipeline

ladder.title: Head of Product / Head of BD
Head of Product / Head of Business

tracks.branches: internal platform product, data product, execution product, exchange partnerships, investor relations, corporate development.
tracks.lateral: product → technology; BD → corp dev; product → COO office; BD → CEO office.
tracks.failure_modes: building for imaginary users; roadmap theater; BD deals that create operational debt; product managers without decision rights; measuring activity instead of outcomes.
tracks.promotion_evidence: shipped a product with measurable adoption; closed a partnership with measurable economics; built a prioritization process others follow.

narrative.text: learn the internal customer. Sit with researchers and traders; understand what makes their day hard. For BD, learn the exchange and vendor landscape.
own a product or a partnership. Ship something used daily; close a deal that saves or earns real money.
own a portfolio. Prioritize ruthlessly. Build a roadmap that the desks trust.
set the agenda and lead. Product strategy, build-vs-buy, commercial negotiations, partner management.
own the function. Represent the firm externally; shape the platform and partnership strategy.

modifiers.notes: Paid for strategy impact, not just papers; research bonus pool tied to strategy P&L
Largest upside and downside; PnL share with high-water mark and deferral
Compete with big tech; equity/LTIP for L5+; on-call premium
Independence requires not tying pay to desk P&L
Firm performance pool, not desk P&L
BD commissions or deal-linked bonus where appropriate

comp.formula:
Desk bonus pool = Share% × max(0, RiskAdjustedPnL − Hurdle − Costs)
Trader bonus    = Pool × IndividualWeight × DeferralFactor
DeferralFactor  = 1 − DeferralRate (vesting over 3–4 years)
principles: Pay for scope and impact, not title. The band sets the range; the contribution sets the position in the range.
Risk-adjust variable pay. PnL share is calculated on risk-adjusted, cost-adjusted, and (where relevant) drawdown-adjusted P&L.
Defer a meaningful share above L4. Deferral aligns time horizons and protects the firm against blow-ups.
No pay for luck. A trader in a beta-driven year should not be paid like an alpha generator. Use peer-relative and risk-adjusted measures.
Transparency in structure, confidentiality in amounts. Everyone should know how comp works; individual numbers stay private.

glossary.meaning: The firm-wide level (L0–L9) that standardizes scope, autonomy, and comp across tracks.
A functional career path (research, trading, technology, etc.) with its own titles and competencies.
A small trading or research team (3–8 people) with a clear mandate and P&L or research ownership.
A group of 2–5 pods under a desk head, with an aggregate P&L and capital budget.
The person accountable for a book or strategy pod's P&L and risk.
Quantitative Researcher / Trader / Developer — the three core IC archetypes.
The individual-contributor path (Staff/Principal) that runs parallel to management.
The principle that IC and management paths are equally prestigious and compensated.
The cross-team process that ensures a band means the same thing everywhere.
The number of direct reports; healthy range for a manager is 5–8, for a desk head 3–5 pods.
Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed — a decision-rights matrix.
Excess return not explained by market exposure.
Excess return divided by volatility; the core risk-adjusted performance measure.
Excess return divided by downside deviation; penalizes only downside volatility.
Peak-to-trough decline in P&L or NAV.
The amount of capital a strategy can deploy before returns degrade materially.
The erosion of a signal's predictive power over time or as more capital uses it.
Trading volume relative to capital; drives costs and capacity.
The difference between expected and realized execution price.
Total cost of executing an order vs the decision price, including market impact and delay.
Volume- or time-weighted average price execution benchmarks.
A trader's place in the limit order book; critical for fill probability.
The risk that a counterparty trades against you precisely when you are wrong.
Quoting two-sided prices to earn the spread while managing inventory.
The risk of holding a position while quoting or executing.
Time from receiving a market-data tick to sending an order.
Placing servers physically close to an exchange's matching engine to reduce latency.
Networking techniques (e.g., DPDK, Solarflare) that skip the OS network stack for lower latency.
Field-programmable gate array; hardware used for ultra-low-latency market-data and order processing.
Order Management System / Execution Management System.
Value at Risk; a quantile loss estimate over a horizon and confidence level.
Average loss beyond the VaR threshold; more tail-sensitive than VaR.
Scenario analysis of portfolio losses under extreme but plausible market moves.
The risk of loss from incorrect or misused models.
Independent review of a model's conceptual soundness, data, calibration, and limitations.
Limits and checks applied before an order is sent to the market.
Tiered risk limits (firm → desk → strategy → operational) with owners and enforcement points.
A control that immediately halts trading for a strategy, desk, or the firm.
Incident severity levels with defined response and communication requirements.
Mean time to recovery/restore.
Service Level Objective / Indicator, and the tolerated failure budget.
The percentage of production changes that cause an incident or rollback.
The documented path of data from source to use, including transformations.
A system that serves consistent feature definitions to research and production.
Practices and tooling for deploying, monitoring, and governing ML models.
Decomposing profit and loss by strategy, desk, instrument, and risk factor.
The minimum return required before profits are shared or capital is allocated.
The peak value that must be recovered before new performance fees/bonuses accrue.
Holding back a portion of variable comp to vest over future years.
Recovering previously paid comp after a restatement, breach, or misconduct.
Paid notice period during which a departing employee is not permitted to work.
Contractual restrictions on joining competitors or poaching colleagues; enforceability varies.
Long-term incentive plan, often tied to firm value or fund profits.
A contractual right to a share of value without actual ownership.
Request for Proposal; used in vendor and partnership selection.
Transaction Cost Analysis; measuring execution quality vs benchmarks.
Formal testing required by an exchange before a member can connect or deploy algorithms.
Events like splits, dividends, mergers, and symbol changes that affect positions and data.
A mismatch between internal records and broker/exchange/custodian records.
The post-trade process of transferring securities and cash, and the counterparty guarantee in between.
A bank that provides financing, custody, and settlement services to a trading firm.
The risk that a trading partner, broker, or exchange defaults.
The risk of being unable to fund or exit positions at a reasonable price.
Monitoring for market abuse, manipulation, and policy violations.
The obligation (where applicable) to obtain the best possible result for client orders.
Major regulatory regimes/frameworks; obligations vary by jurisdiction and entity.
US Federal Reserve guidance on model risk management; widely used as a reference standard.

checklists.title: The manager's monthly checklist
items: One skip-level conversation per direct report's team
Review desk/team P&L or SLOs with the team, not just the numbers
Check open risk findings and incident actions
Review hiring pipeline and at least one interview
Identify one person ready for more scope and one at risk of stagnation
Read one research memo or design doc end-to-end
Ask: what decision is stuck, and who owns it?

checklists.title: The CEO's quarterly checklist
items: Capital allocation review by desk and strategy
Talent review: L5+ bench, succession, retention risks
Technology and platform roadmap review with CTO
Regulatory and compliance standing with CCO/GC
Financial position and funding with CFO
One external relationship deepened (investor, exchange, regulator, academic)
One thing stopped (strategy, project, vendor, process)

rows: (Return − risk-free) / volatility, net of costs, annualized
Rolling IC or Sharpe trend of a live signal
Strategies reaching G4 / ideas at G1
Actions closed on time / total actions
Lag between event time and availability
Production datasets with documented lineage / total
High performers lost / total high performers
Promotions filled internally / total L4+ hires

search.title: How to use this document
search.text: How to use this document This is the operating manual for how a quant trading firm is structured, how people grow, and how decisions get made. It is written for three audiences: Founders / CEO: the target org, the C-suite design, the governance and capital-allocation machinery. Managers / Heads of Desk / Heads of Function: the level definitions, promotion gates, KPIs, and hiring bars you will apply. Individual contributors (QR, QT, QD, data, risk, ops): the journey map for your track — what "next level" actually means, and the evidence required. Three rules for reading it: Levels are scope, not seniority theater. A level describes what you own, what you may decide alone, and over what horizon — not how long you've been around. Titles are local; bands are universal. Every firm names things differently. The L0–L9 bands let you compare a Senior QR at an HFT prop shop with a VP at a bank and a Staff engineer at a big-tech firm. The map is not the territory. Use the journeys as a default, then adapt to your firm's strategy, market, and regulatory footprint. Scope note (per brief): HR and HR-adjacent job families (recruiting, talent, people ops, L&D, benefits/compensation administration, HRBPs) are excluded.

search.title: How to use this document
search.text: People processes — promotion calibration, compensation philosophy, performance reviews — remain, because they are manager and CEO responsibilities and cannot be separated from a career framework.

search.title: The <100-person algo trading firm
search.text: The <100-person algo trading firm The reference organization is the attached chart: a CEO over five pillars — HR & Operations, Strategies, Research, Technology, Risk & Compliance — with roughly 40–60 people in the core value chain. Reading the chart correctly: Strategies is the commercial engine: four small trading teams, each a mix of traders, QRs, QDs, and C++ engineers. Each team is a proto-P&L pod. Research is the factory that feeds Strategies: ML, portfolio optimization, and market microstructure are shared research capabilities, not desk-owned. Technology is split between infrastructure/co-location (the latency backbone) and software (the application layer). Risk & Compliance is deliberately independent of Strategies — the person who can say "no" to the desk must not report to the desk. HR & Operations combines two very different functions. Per the brief, HR is excluded from this framework; Operations is retained and expanded as its own pillar. The color legend in the source chart maps people to role families: traders, quant researchers, quant developers, software engineers, C++ engineers, risk analysts. In this document we generalize those into tracks with full ladders. What the chart gets right (keep it): Small, autonomous trading teams with clear ownership. Research as a shared capability, not a cost center. Risk independent from trading.

search.title: The <100-person algo trading firm
search.text: A flat span of control (CEO → Head → Lead → IC). What the chart leaves implicit (this document makes explicit): How an intern becomes a Head of Desk. What separates a Senior QR from a Staff QR. Who owns capital allocation, model deployment, and incidents. How the firm scales past 100 without turning into a bank.

search.text: Scaling stages: 100–250 and 250–500 Dimension <100 (current) 100–250 (scale-up) 250–500 (multi-pod / multi-office) --- --- --- --- C-suite CEO + 4–6 heads; some player-coaches CEO + CTO, CRO, CFO, COO, CCO/GC; CDO emerging Full C-suite + Chief Scientist, CISO, CBO/CSO; regional heads Trading 4 desk pods, one Head of Strategies 8–15 pods, 2–3 desk heads, central risk Multi-strat pods, PMs with capital budgets, independent risk Research One Head of Research, 3 sub-leads Research pods aligned to horizons; research engineering Central research + desk-embedded researchers; formal model risk Technology Infra + software + co-lo, ~10–20 engineers Platform teams, SRE, security, dedicated low-latency group Multi-site, hardware lab, formal architecture review board Data Data engineering embedded in tech Dedicated data platform + ML engineering Data mesh / lakehouse, governance, lineage, CDO Risk 2–4 risk analysts, Head of Risk Market/credit/liquidity split, model validation Independent model risk, stress testing, scenario library Compliance/Legal Combined Head of Risk & Compliance Separate Compliance + Legal CCO + GC + surveillance + regulatory affairs Finance Outsourced accounting + CFO-as-needed Full finance team, treasury Treasury desk, FP&A, tax, capital planning Operations Trade ops + exchange connectivity Dedicated market ops, corporate actions 24/6 global ops, incident command Product/Business Product managers for internal tools Product + exchange partnerships Product org + investor relations + corp dev The scaling rule: add a management layer only when a Head is managing more than ~7 people or more than 2 distinct workflows.

search.title: Scaling stages: 100–250 and 250–500
search.text: Add a C-suite role only when the function has firm-wide decision rights (capital, risk, technology architecture, regulatory). Otherwise, keep it as a Head-of-Function at L6.

search.title: Ten design principles
search.text: Ten design principles P&L proximity, not P&L theater. Every role should be able to point to the number it moves: net Sharpe, latency percentile, reconciliation break rate, validation finding severity. Support functions measure risk avoided and capacity created, not activity. Small autonomous pods with shared rails. Trading teams own their strategies; research, data, and infrastructure are shared platforms so pods don't rebuild the same wheels. Risk has a veto, not a vote. The CRO can block a strategy launch or limit increase; the desk can escalate to the CEO, but cannot override unilaterally. One ladder, many tracks. A Senior QR, Senior QT, and Senior QD sit at the same band and should be comparable in scope, compensation logic, and promotion rigor. Dual track is real. Staff/Principal ICs are not "failed managers." They are the technical spine of the firm and are paid accordingly. Promotion is evidence-based and calibrated. No level is granted for tenure; every promotion has a written packet, a sponsor, and a calibration committee. Separation of duties. Research proposes, risk validates, execution deploys, finance reconciles. No single person owns the whole chain for a live strategy. Information flows to the decision. The person closest to the data makes the call, within explicit limits; escalation is for exceptions, not routine approvals.

search.title: Ten design principles
search.text: Latency and reliability are product features. Technology is not a cost center; it is the execution edge. SRE and low-latency engineers sit at the same table as traders. Scale the organization, not the bureaucracy. Every new process must replace a worse process or remove a bottleneck. If it only adds control, it needs a sunset clause.

search.title: Research & Strategy
search.text: Research & Strategy Mission: convert data into repeatable, risk-adjusted predictive signals and portfolio decisions. Role One-line scope Primary interfaces Typical bands --- --- --- --- Quantitative Researcher (QR) / Alpha Researcher Builds statistical, econometric, and ML models to predict short-term price moves and microstructure signals Data, QD, QT, risk L1–L8 Execution / Microstructure Researcher Studies order-book dynamics, queue position, slippage, optimal routing Execution traders, low-latency engineers, exchange connectivity L2–L7 Data Quant / Alternative Data Researcher Sources, cleans, and models tick data, order books, news, and alternative datasets Data engineering, compliance (vendor licensing) L1–L7 ML Researcher (added) Develops deep learning, representation learning, and NLP models for alpha and regime detection QR, data/ML platform L2–L8 Portfolio Optimization Researcher (added) Turns raw signals into portfolio weights under risk, cost, and capacity constraints QR, risk, treasury L2–L8 Research Engineer (added) Builds the research platform: backtesting, feature stores, experiment tracking, reproducibility QD, data platform L1–L6 What the domain owns: the research agenda, the signal library, the backtesting standard, the research review cadence, and the "kill list" of dead ideas.

search.title: Research & Strategy
search.text: What good looks like: Every signal has a documented hypothesis, data lineage, out-of-sample protocol, capacity estimate, and decay monitoring. Research review is adversarial but blameless: the goal is to kill weak ideas cheaply. A QR can explain why a signal should work, not just that it backtested well. Interfaces and handoffs: Research → Strategies: a signal graduates through a signal readiness review (documentation, OOS results, capacity, risk limits). Research → Technology: production requirements (latency, data volume, update frequency). Research → Risk: model assumptions and failure modes. Common failure modes: backtest overfitting, data leakage, ignoring transaction costs, signals that work only in one regime, research that never ships.

search.title: Trading & Portfolio Management
search.text: Trading & Portfolio Management Mission: deploy capital profitably and safely in live markets, and manage the risk of the book in real time. Role One-line scope Primary interfaces Typical bands --- --- --- --- Quantitative Trader (QT) Runs live strategies, monitors risk and P&L, tunes parameters, manages intraday/short-horizon exposures QR, QD, risk, ops L1–L8 Execution Trader Low-impact order execution, liquidity provision, market making across exchanges Microstructure research, low-latency tech, exchange connectivity L1–L7 Portfolio Manager (PM) / Quant PM Owns P&L for a book or strategy pod, allocates capital and risk limits, leads researchers/traders CEO/CRO, desk heads, research L4–L8 Market Maker (added) Quotes two-sided markets, manages inventory and adverse selection Execution tech, risk, microstructure research L1–L7 Desk Head (added) Runs a desk of 2–5 pods; owns aggregate P&L and capital deployment within limits Head of Strategies, CRO, CFO L5–L7 What the domain owns: live P&L, fill quality, inventory, execution costs, strategy parameter tuning, and the trading calendar. What good looks like: Traders know their risk budget and capacity as precisely as their P&L. Execution is measured against a benchmark (arrival price, VWAP, implementation shortfall) — not just "did it fill." A trader can explain the strategy's edge, its failure regime, and the kill switch.

search.title: Trading & Portfolio Management
search.text: Interfaces: Strategies ↔ Research (signal handoff), Strategies ↔ Risk (limits, stress), Strategies ↔ Ops (connectivity, corporate actions), Strategies ↔ Finance (P&L attribution, treasury). Common failure modes: overriding risk limits in the heat of the moment, position sizing by conviction instead of risk, ignoring capacity, mistaking beta for alpha, revenge trading after a drawdown.

search.title: Software, Low-Latency & Hardware Engineering
search.text: Software, Low-Latency & Hardware Engineering Mission: turn research and trading logic into fast, reliable, observable production systems — and keep them running when markets misbehave. Role One-line scope Primary interfaces Typical bands --- --- --- --- Quantitative Developer (QD) Production code for models, pricing, backtesting, and trading logic (C++, Rust, Python) QR, QT, platform L1–L8 Low-Latency / HFT Systems Engineer Kernel bypass, networking, lock-free concurrency, tick-to-trade latency Co-location, exchange connectivity, traders L2–L8 FPGA / Hardware Engineer Verilog/VHDL/FPGA for market-data decoding and order execution Low-latency, exchanges, hardware vendors L2–L8 Core / Infrastructure / SRE / DevOps Engineer Distributed compute, simulation/backtesting pipelines, telemetry, production reliability Everyone L1–L8 Security Engineer (added) Application security, secrets, access control, incident response CTO, compliance, ops L2–L7 Build / Release Engineer (added) CI/CD, reproducible builds, deployment orchestration QD, SRE L1–L6 What the domain owns: the production platform, latency SLOs, uptime, deployment safety, observability, and the technology roadmap. What good looks like: p99 latency and jitter are tracked like P&L; regressions trigger alerts, not post-mortems a week later. Every production change is reproducible, reversible, and tested in simulation.

search.title: Software, Low-Latency & Hardware Engineering
search.text: On-call is humane: alerts are actionable, runbooks exist, and incidents produce fixes, not blame. Interfaces: Technology ↔ Research (research compute, backtesting), Technology ↔ Trading (execution, market data), Technology ↔ Risk (risk checks in the order path), Technology ↔ Ops (connectivity, exchange certifications). Common failure modes: optimizing the wrong percentile, hero-driven operations, untested failover, configuration drift, "it works on my machine" deployments.

search.title: Data, Risk & Control
search.text: Data, Risk & Control Mission: make data trustworthy, make risk visible, and make the control environment independent. Role One-line scope Primary interfaces Typical bands --- --- --- --- Data Engineer / Machine Learning Engineer Petabyte-scale tick storage, feature pipelines, ML training infrastructure Research, technology, compliance L1–L8 Quantitative Risk Manager / Risk Engineer Real-time exposure, stress tests, tail risk, margin/position limits, model validation Trading, research, finance L1–L8 Model Validation Quant Independently tests pricing, risk, and statistical assumptions for accuracy and robustness Research, risk, compliance L2–L7 Market Risk Analyst (added) Monitors delta/vega/gamma, concentration, liquidity, and scenario P&L Desk, risk L1–L6 Credit / Counterparty Risk Analyst (added) Exchange, prime broker, and counterparty exposure Treasury, risk, legal L1–L6 Liquidity Risk Analyst (added) Funding liquidity, margin calls, stress liquidity Treasury, risk L1–L6 Compliance / Surveillance Analyst (added) Trade surveillance, market-abuse monitoring, regulatory reporting Compliance, legal, trading L1–L7 What the domain owns: the risk framework, limits, stress library, data quality SLAs, and independent validation. What good looks like: Risk limits are pre-trade, not post-hoc reports.

search.title: Data, Risk & Control
search.text: Every model has an independent validation memo with assumptions, limitations, and failure modes. Data has lineage, freshness SLAs, and reconciliation against exchange records. Compliance can reconstruct any order's lifecycle from immutable logs. Interfaces: Risk ↔ Trading (limits, stress), Risk ↔ Research (model assumptions), Data ↔ everyone, Compliance ↔ trading/legal/regulators. Common failure modes: risk reports that arrive after the loss, stale data silently used in production, validation that rubber-stamps, compliance treated as a paperwork function.

search.title: Operations & Corporate Functions
search.text: Operations & Corporate Functions Mission: keep the firm's plumbing working — connectivity, settlements, reconciliations, treasury, accounting, legal — so the front office can focus on markets. Role One-line scope Primary interfaces Typical bands --- --- --- --- Trading Operations / Market Ops Exchange connectivity, corporate actions, reconciliations, live incident response Trading, technology, exchanges L1–L7 Compliance, Legal & Finance Regulatory reporting, exchange rules, treasury, firm accounting CEO, risk, regulators L1–L8 Treasury Analyst / Dealer (added) Cash, collateral, margin, FX, funding CFO, risk, prime brokers L1–L7 Financial Analyst / Controller (added) P&L attribution, month-end close, tax, audit CFO, trading, ops L1–L7 Corporate Development / Strategy (added) Partnerships, acquisitions, exchange deals, new-market entry CEO, CFO, legal L2–L7 Office of the CEO / Chief of Staff (added) Cross-functional execution, board materials, special projects CEO, C-suite L3–L7 What the domain owns: operational reliability, regulatory standing, financial integrity, and corporate infrastructure. What good looks like: Reconciliations break rarely; when they do, they are resolved same-day with root cause. Exchange certifications and rule changes are tracked ahead of deadlines. The books close on time and P&L is attributable to strategy, desk, and instrument.

search.title: Operations & Corporate Functions
search.text: Legal and compliance are consulted before new products launch, not after. Interfaces: Ops ↔ Trading/Tech (connectivity, incidents), Finance ↔ all (P&L, budgets), Legal/Compliance ↔ product and trading (new markets, licensing), Corp Dev ↔ CEO/CFO. Common failure modes: manual processes that only one person understands, reconciliation debt, regulatory surprises, treasury surprises on margin calls.

search.title: Product & Business (new)
search.text: Product & Business (new) Mission: make the firm's internal platforms usable and its external commercial relationships productive. Role One-line scope Primary interfaces Typical bands --- --- --- --- Product Manager (internal platforms) Owns the roadmap for research, execution, and data platforms; translates desk needs into product requirements Research, tech, trading L2–L7 Business Development / Exchange Partnerships Negotiates connectivity, fee schedules, market-data licenses, and strategic partnerships CEO, CFO, legal, ops L2–L8 Investor Relations / Capital Raising (scaled firm) Manages LP relationships, fundraising, and reporting CEO, CFO, compliance L4–L8 Chief Business Officer / Chief Strategy Officer (scaled firm) Owns corporate strategy, partnerships, and growth CEO, C-suite L8 What the domain owns: platform adoption, commercial terms, strategic partnerships, and (when applicable) capital relationships. What good looks like: Product decisions are backed by usage data and desk interviews, not opinion. Exchange and vendor economics are renegotiated on a schedule, not when a contract expires. External partners see one firm, not five competing internal voices. Interfaces: Product ↔ tech/research/trading; BD ↔ CEO/CFO/legal/ops; IR ↔ CEO/CFO/compliance.

search.title: Product & Business (new)
search.text: Common failure modes: product managers without decision rights, BD deals that create operational debt, IR promises the firm cannot operationally deliver.

search.title: Why one ladder
search.text: Why one ladder Firms usually have three incompatible ladders: researchers get "Senior → Staff," traders get "Junior → Senior → PM," engineers get "L3 → L8." That makes compensation arguments incoherent and lets a "VP" at a bank outrank a "Head of Desk" at a prop shop on paper while doing less. The unified ladder fixes this with one currency: scope × autonomy × impact horizon × decision rights. Titles still vary by track; the band does not. Every band answers five questions: What do you own? (task → module → strategy → desk → function → firm) What can you decide alone? (execute → propose → own → allocate → govern) Over what horizon? (days → weeks → months → quarters → years) Whom do you grow? (self → juniors → project teams → managers → the firm) What evidence proves you're ready for the next band?

search.title: The ten bands at a glance
search.text: The ten bands at a glance Band Firm-facing title Owns Autonomy Horizon People Comp shape --- --- --- --- --- --- --- L0 Intern / Summer Analyst An assigned task Supervised Days–weeks — Stipend L1 Analyst / Associate A project component Guided Weeks — Base + bonus L2 Quant / Trader / Engineer A signal, module, or book slice Independent Weeks–months Mentors juniors Base + bonus L3 Senior QR / QT / QD A strategy, system, or desk function Sets own priorities Months Leads projects Base + bonus + impact award L4 Staff / Principal / Desk Lead A platform or multi-strategy cluster Sets direction Quarters Leads 3–10 ICs + PnL share / equity L5 Manager / Head of Desk Desk P&L + team Allocates within limits Quarters–years Manages ICs PnL share + equity L6 Director / Head of Function A function (research, tech, risk…) Owns function strategy Years Manages managers Profit pool + equity L7 VP / SVP / Deputy C-Suite A firm-wide domain Sets firm policy Years Org-wide influence Equity L8 C-Suite The firm (CEO-1) CEO-1 authority Years Whole function Equity + LTIP L9 CEO The firm Board-level Multi-year The firm Equity Two important calibrations: L4 is a real fork. Staff/Principal ICs and Desk Leads both sit here. One scales technical depth; the other scales people and P&L. Neither is "above" the other. L7 is a bridge band.

search.title: The ten bands at a glance
search.text: It exists so a Deputy CTO or SVP Research can own a firm-wide domain without being on the executive team. In a <100-person firm, L7 may be empty; in a 250+ firm, it is where regional heads and deputies live.

search.title: The ten bands at a glance
search.heading: The original seven-rank ladder (preserved)
search.text: The firm's original taxonomy is retained below, close to verbatim. The right-hand column maps each rank to the unified band so the old language and the new ladder can coexist. "Exact titles vary by firm, but most HFT and quant shops follow a flat-to-tiered meritocratic ladder tied closely to P&L or technical impact." Intern / Summer Analyst: Short-term research, trading simulation, or coding projects; primary pipeline for full-time offers. → L0 Junior / Associate / Analyst (Entry-Level, ~0–2 yrs): Executes defined research tasks, builds basic tools, or assists on live trading desks under supervision. → L1 Mid-Level Quant / Trader / Developer (~2–5 yrs): Independently owns signals, trading books, or core low-latency systems. → L2 Senior Quant / Senior Trader / Senior Engineer (~5+ yrs): Leads complex strategies or mission-critical infrastructure and mentors junior staff. → L3 Vice President (VP) / Director / Principal: Used more often at banks and larger multi-strat funds; denotes high technical or desk authority. → L4–L6, calibrated by scope (a bank VP is often L4; a Director is L5–L6) Portfolio Manager (PM) / Head of Desk: Runs a standalone profit center or team with explicit capital and risk budgets. → L5 Managing Director (MD) / Partner / C-Suite (CEO, CTO, CRO, Head of Quant): Shapes firm-wide strategy, capital allocation, risk governance, and leadership.

search.title: The ten bands at a glance
search.heading: The original seven-rank ladder (preserved)
search.text: → L7–L9 Why the mapping is not one-to-one: the original ladder mixes technical seniority (Principal), bank hierarchy (VP, Director, MD), and P&L ownership (PM, Head of Desk). The unified bands separate those dimensions, so a "VP" and a "Head of Desk" can be compared on scope rather than title. This is also why the title-translation matrix in §13 matters: it lets you hire laterally without importing someone else's hierarchy by accident.

search.title: Band-by-band definitions
search.heading: L0 — Intern / Summer Analyst
search.text: Mission: prove you can learn fast, work with data, and communicate clearly. Scope: one well-defined project with a named supervisor and a written brief. Autonomy: supervised; you ask before changing direction. Deliverables: a working analysis, notebook, or tool; a short presentation; a written handoff. What "good" looks like: the work is reproducible, the conclusion is honest, and the intern can explain why the method was chosen. Promotion signal: an offer to return at L1 — not because the project succeeded, but because the reasoning and collaboration were sound. Common titles: Summer Analyst, Research Intern, Trading Intern, Software Engineering Intern.

search.title: Band-by-band definitions
search.heading: L1 — Analyst / Associate (entry level, ~0–2 years)
search.text: Mission: execute defined work reliably and start forming judgment. Scope: a component of a larger project — a data pipeline, a backtest module, a risk report, a reconciliation. Autonomy: guided; the supervisor sets the what, you own the how within agreed bounds. Impact horizon: weeks. Deliverables: clean code/analysis, documented assumptions, on-time delivery, clear status updates. Decision rights: none over capital or production; may propose improvements. Promotion signal: consistent independent delivery, correct use of statistical/engineering fundamentals, and evidence of why not just what. Common titles: Analyst, Associate, Junior Quant, Junior Trader, Graduate Engineer.

search.title: Band-by-band definitions
search.heading: L2 — Quant / Trader / Engineer (mid level, ~2–4 years)
search.text: Mission: own a meaningful piece of the machine end-to-end. Scope: one signal, one execution module, one risk model, one platform service, or a slice of a book. Autonomy: independent on day-to-day decisions; escalates design changes and limit exceptions. Impact horizon: weeks–months.
