Deliverables: a production-quality signal/system with tests, monitoring, documentation; a measurable contribution to P&L, latency, uptime, or risk coverage. Decision rights: may deploy within sandbox/limits; may approve small technical changes; cannot change firm risk limits. People: mentors L0–L1; reviews peers' code/analysis. Promotion signal: owns outcomes, not tasks; handles ambiguity; their work is used by others without rework. Common titles: Quant Researcher, Quant Trader, Quant Developer, Software Engineer, Data Engineer, Risk Analyst.

search.title: Band-by-band definitions
search.heading: L3 — Senior (QR / QT / QD), ~4–7 years
search.text: Mission: own a strategy, system, or function that materially moves the firm's numbers. Scope: a full strategy from hypothesis to production, a critical platform, or a desk function (execution, risk coverage, data platform). Autonomy: sets own priorities within the mandate; makes technical calls; represents the firm in their domain. Impact horizon: months. Deliverables: strategy P&L or platform SLOs; a documented research/engineering agenda; mentorship of L1–L2; cross-team design reviews. Decision rights: can approve production changes in their domain; can spend within a small budget; can veto unsafe technical choices (with escalation path). People: leads projects and 1–3 juniors; not yet a people manager. Promotion signal: repeatable success across more than one project; influence beyond their own work; ability to say "no" with evidence. Common titles: Senior Quant Researcher, Senior Trader, Senior Software Engineer, Senior Data Engineer, Senior Risk Analyst.

search.title: Band-by-band definitions
search.heading: L4 — Staff / Principal / Desk Lead (~7–10 years)
search.text: Mission: multiply other people's output — through architecture, strategy, or desk leadership. Scope: a platform, a multi-strategy cluster, a research program, or a desk of 2–5 pods. Autonomy: sets direction for the area; negotiates priorities with L5+; owns technical or trading standards. Impact horizon: quarters. Deliverables: platform roadmap or strategy cluster P&L; standards, tooling, and reviews that raise the whole team; a pipeline of L2–L3 talent. Decision rights: allocates technical resources within the area; approves designs; may own a small P&L or cost center. People: leads 3–10 ICs (directly or matrixed); coaches L3s. Promotion signal: the area runs better because you exist; you are the person others consult before a major decision; you have built something that outlives your direct involvement. Common titles: Staff Quant Researcher, Principal Engineer, Staff Data Engineer, Desk Lead, Research Lead.

search.title: Band-by-band definitions
search.heading: L5 — Manager / Head of Desk
search.text: Mission: own a P&L and the team that produces it. Scope: a desk (2–5 pods) or a function with a clear mandate and budget. Autonomy: allocates capital within risk limits; hires/fires (with calibration); sets desk strategy. Impact horizon: quarters–years. Deliverables: risk-adjusted P&L; team development; capacity and cost management; strategy pipeline. Decision rights: capital allocation within limits, position limits within CRO-approved bands, compensation recommendations, vendor spend within budget. People: manages ICs and L4 leads; builds the bench. Promotion signal: sustained P&L through different regimes; a team that performs without you in the room; clean risk and compliance record; succession plan in place. Common titles: Head of Desk, Trading Manager, Research Manager, Engineering Manager, Risk Manager.

search.title: Band-by-band definitions
search.heading: L6 — Director / Head of Function
search.text: Mission: own a function's strategy and its interface with the rest of the firm. Scope: Research, Technology, Risk, Data, Finance, Operations, Compliance, or Product — multiple teams and managers. Autonomy: sets function strategy; owns the budget; represents the function at the executive table. Impact horizon: years. Deliverables: function roadmap; talent strategy; cross-functional agreements (SLAs, risk appetite, tech standards); regulatory standing. Decision rights: function budget, org design, vendor selection, prioritization; co-owns firm-level decisions with C-suite. People: manages managers; develops L5 successors. Promotion signal: the function is a competitive advantage, not a support center; peers trust the function's judgment; you can run the firm's agenda in your domain. Common titles: Head of Research, Head of Technology, Head of Risk, Head of Data, Head of Finance, Head of Operations, Head of Compliance, Director.

search.title: Band-by-band definitions
search.heading: L7 — VP / SVP / Deputy C-Suite
search.text: Mission: own a firm-wide domain or a major sub-function at scale. Scope: a domain that spans teams and geographies — e.g., Global Execution, Research Platform, Risk Analytics, Treasury, Legal. Autonomy: sets policy within the C-suite's mandate; acts for the C-suite officer when delegated. Impact horizon: years. Deliverables: firm-wide standards, multi-year roadmap, regulatory relationships, major change programs. Decision rights: delegated authority from a C-suite officer; represents the firm externally in the domain. People: leads L6 managers; shapes the leadership pipeline. Promotion signal: trusted to run the domain without supervision; external recognition; succession-ready for L8. Common titles: SVP Engineering, VP Risk, Deputy CTO, Global Head of Execution, Head of Legal.

search.title: Band-by-band definitions
search.heading: L8 — C-Suite (CEO-1)
search.text: Mission: own a firm-wide function and its contribution to firm strategy. Scope: Technology, Risk, Finance, Operations, Compliance/Legal, Data, Research, Trading, or Business — depending on the firm's structure. Autonomy: full functional authority; co-owns firm strategy with the CEO and peers. Impact horizon: years. Deliverables: functional strategy, capital/risk/tech agenda, regulatory relationships, leadership bench, board reporting. Decision rights: function budget and org; firm-level policies in the domain; veto rights where the domain requires independence (CRO, CCO). People: leads the function's leadership team; develops L7 successors. Promotion signal: the board and CEO trust the function's judgment; the function is audit-clean and strategy-aligned; a credible successor exists. Common titles: CTO, CRO, CFO, COO, CCO, General Counsel, CDO, Chief Scientist, Head of Strategies/Chief Trading Officer.

search.title: Band-by-band definitions
search.heading: L9 — CEO
search.text: Mission: set the firm's strategy, allocate capital across businesses, and own the final trade-off between risk and return. Scope: the entire firm — strategy, capital, people, culture, regulatory standing, board and investor relationships. Autonomy: board-level; accountable to shareholders/partners. Impact horizon: multi-year. Deliverables: firm strategy and capital plan; executive team; risk appetite; external relationships; succession. Decision rights: final call on capital allocation, M&A, new businesses, C-suite appointments (with board), and firm-wide risk appetite. People: leads the C-suite; builds the next CEO. Succession signal: a board-approved successor and a firm that can run without the founder in the room. Common titles: CEO, Managing Partner, Founder-CEO.

search.title: Title translation matrix
search.text: Title translation matrix Band HFT / prop firm Multi-strat / hedge fund Investment bank Big tech Crypto / fintech --- --- --- --- --- --- L0 Intern Summer Analyst Summer Analyst Intern Intern L1 Analyst / Junior Quant Analyst Analyst L3 / Junior Analyst L2 Quant / Trader / Engineer Associate Associate / VP-track L4 Quant / Engineer L3 Senior QR/QT/QD Senior Analyst / Junior PM VP L5 Senior L4 Staff / Principal / Desk Lead Senior PM / Pod Lead Director L6 (Staff) Staff / Lead L5 Head of Desk PM / Desk Head Managing Director L7 (Manager) Head of Desk L6 Head of Function Head of Strategy / COO MD / Head of Desk L8 (Senior Manager) Head of Function L7 SVP / Deputy C-suite Sector Head / COO MD / Global Head L9 (Director) VP / SVP L8 CTO/CRO/CFO/COO/CCO C-suite / Partner C-suite / MD VP / SVP C-suite L9 CEO CIO / Managing Partner CEO CEO CEO How to use the matrix: when hiring laterally, map the candidate's scope and decision rights — not their title — to a band. A bank VP with 30 approvals a day is not automatically an L3; a big-tech Staff engineer who has never touched a P&L may be an L4 technically but an L3 commercially. Calibrate with the band questions in §10.

search.title: Time-in-level and promotion philosophy
search.text: Time-in-level and promotion philosophy Band Typical time in level Promotion cadence "Up or stay" expectation --- --- --- --- L0 10–12 weeks End of internship Return offer or exit L1 18–30 months Annual Up to L2 or exit L2 24–36 months Annual Up to L3 or specialize L3 30–48 months Semi-annual Up to L4, or stay as senior IC L4 3–5 years Semi-annual Up to L5, or remain Staff/Principal (no penalty) L5 3–5 years Annual Up to L6, or remain a strong desk head L6 3–5 years Annual Up to L7/C-suite, or remain a function head L7 3–5 years Annual C-suite or senior IC/advisor L8 5+ years Board cycle CEO or board/advisor L9 — Board Succession Three rules that prevent title inflation: No promotion without a written packet (Appendix C) and a calibration committee. No level change without a scope change. If the job is the same, it's a compensation discussion, not a promotion. Staying is a valid career. L4 Staff/Principal and L5 Head of Desk are terminal-by-choice levels with full comp and respect. Not everyone should be pushed into management. The "up or stay" conversation: at every review, the manager must ask: "Do you want the next band, or do you want to deepen this one?" Both answers are legitimate. The firm's job is to make the deep-IC path as prestigious and well-paid as the management path.

search.title: Research track (QR / ML / microstructure / alt-data / portfolio optimization)
search.text: Research track (QR / ML / microstructure / alt-data / portfolio optimization) Entry points: PhD or Master's in statistics, ML, mathematics, physics, CS, economics; exceptional undergraduates with research evidence; internships converted from L0. Lateral hires from other funds, banks, or big-tech research.

search.title: Research track (QR / ML / microstructure / alt-data / portfolio optimization)
search.text: Band Title Mission Scope Primary KPIs Promotion gate --- --- --- --- --- --- L0 Research Intern Learn the research process One supervised project Reproducibility, clarity Return offer L1 Research Analyst Execute research components Datasets, backtests, replications Correctness, speed, documentation Independent module delivery L2 Quant Researcher Own a signal end-to-end One signal/strategy component OOS Sharpe, turnover, capacity, decay Signal survives readiness review + live L3 Senior QR Own a strategy family Multiple signals, one research agenda Net Sharpe of family, research-to-prod conversion Repeatable success across ≥2 ideas L4 Staff / Principal QR Set research methodology Multi-strategy program, standards Firm-wide research quality, replication rate Methodology adopted beyond own team L5 Research Manager / Head of Pod Lead researchers + research P&L 3–10 researchers Team output, talent pipeline Team performs without you L6 Head of Research Own the research function All research pods, budget, hiring bar Function strategy, model risk standing Function is a competitive advantage L7 Chief Scientist / SVP Research Firm-wide research agenda External reputation, PhD pipeline, long-horizon bets Breakthroughs, external recognition Board/CEO trust; successor ready L8 C-suite (if structured) Research as a firm pillar Firm strategy with peers Firm-level research edge — Journey narrative.

search.title: Research track (QR / ML / microstructure / alt-data / portfolio optimization)
search.text: Years 0–2 (L0–L1): learn the craft. Reproduce papers, build clean datasets, run honest backtests. The goal is not a great idea; it is not fooling yourself. Master the data, the backtester, and the cost model. Years 2–4 (L2): own one signal from hypothesis to production. Learn why most ideas die: costs, capacity, regime dependence, data leakage. Ship something small and real. Years 4–7 (L3): own a family of signals. Develop taste for which ideas are worth pursuing. Mentor juniors. Present at research review and defend your assumptions. Years 7–10 (L4): set methodology. Build the research platform's standards, the replication protocol, the kill criteria. Your impact is now through other researchers. Years 10+ (L5–L6): lead the function. Balance long-horizon research with near-term P&L; protect research independence from desk pressure; own the hiring bar. Branches: alpha/statistical arbitrage, ML/deep learning, market microstructure, alternative data, portfolio optimization, execution research. Lateral moves: QR → QT (with trading mentorship), QR → model validation (risk), QR → data science/product, QR → research management. Failure modes: overfitting to backtests; never shipping; ignoring transaction costs; single-regime dependence; poor documentation; treating research review as a formality; refusing to kill a dead idea.

search.title: Research track (QR / ML / microstructure / alt-data / portfolio optimization)
search.text: Promotion evidence (L2→L3): two or more signals in production, at least one with 12+ months live attribution; documented OOS protocol; mentorship of an L1; a research review presentation that survived adversarial questioning.

search.title: Trading track (QT / execution / market making / PM)
search.text: Trading track (QT / execution / market making / PM) Entry points: quantitative degrees, internships, prop trading, poker/competitive games, military/ops discipline, lateral hires from other desks. Trading is the most apprenticeship-heavy track; simulation and live mentorship matter more than credentials.

search.title: Trading track (QT / execution / market making / PM)
search.text: Band Title Mission Scope Primary KPIs Promotion gate --- --- --- --- --- --- L0 Trading Intern Learn market mechanics Simulated book / one strategy Risk discipline, game performance Return offer L1 Junior Trader Run a small book under supervision One strategy slice P&L vs risk, limit adherence Independent book over 2+ regimes L2 Quant Trader Own a strategy/book slice One strategy or instrument Net P&L, Sharpe, drawdown, fill quality Consistent risk-adjusted P&L L3 Senior Trader Own a strategy family / desk function Multiple strategies, execution, mentoring Desk P&L, capacity, regime robustness Sustained P&L through a drawdown L4 Desk Lead Lead 2–5 pods Aggregate desk P&L Team P&L, capital efficiency, talent Team performs without you L5 Head of Desk Own desk P&L + team Desk strategy, hiring, risk Risk-adjusted desk P&L, limit record Succession + clean risk record L6 Head of Trading / Strategies Own all desks Capital deployment, strategy pipeline Firm trading P&L, capacity, market entry Firm-level trading edge L7 Chief Trading Officer / SVP Firm-wide trading strategy New markets, execution model Strategic P&L growth C-suite readiness L8 C-suite (Head of Strategies) Trading as a firm pillar Firm strategy with peers Firm-level — Journey narrative. Years 0–2 (L0–L1): learn to not lose money. Risk limits are training wheels, not insults.

search.title: Trading track (QT / execution / market making / PM)
search.text: Master the mechanics: order types, queue, slippage, settlement, corporate actions. Years 2–4 (L2): own a book. Learn position sizing, correlation, and the difference between edge and luck. Survive your first drawdown without changing strategy mid-flight. Years 4–7 (L3): own a strategy family. Adapt across regimes. Mentor juniors. Learn to communicate P&L attribution clearly to risk and management. Years 7–10 (L4–L5): lead a desk. Allocate capital, build a strategy pipeline, manage a team of strong personalities. Your job is now capital allocation and talent, not just trading. Years 10+ (L6–L7): run trading as a business. Decide which markets to enter/exit, how much capital each desk gets, and how the firm's risk appetite evolves. Branches: market making, execution, systematic directional, options/volatility, crypto, cross-asset. Lateral moves: QT → QR (research depth), QT → product/BD (market structure expertise), QT → risk (desk experience is valuable), QT → management. Failure modes: overriding risk limits; increasing size to recover losses; hiding drawdowns; mistaking a bull regime for skill; poor handoffs; burning out on night sessions. Promotion evidence (L2→L3): 12–24 months of positive risk-adjusted P&L through at least one drawdown; zero limit breaches; documented strategy logic; mentorship of an L1; a clear capacity estimate.

search.title: Technology track (QD / low-latency / FPGA / infra / SRE / security)
search.text: Technology track (QD / low-latency / FPGA / infra / SRE / security) Entry points: CS/EE degrees, systems programming, competitive programming, kernel/networking hobbies, FPGA projects, lateral hires from HFT, big tech, or exchanges.

search.title: Technology track (QD / low-latency / FPGA / infra / SRE / security)
search.text: Band Title Mission Scope Primary KPIs Promotion gate --- --- --- --- --- --- L0 Engineering Intern Learn production discipline One module/tool Tests, clarity, review quality Return offer L1 Software Engineer Deliver reliable components One service/module Correctness, latency, on-call Independent ownership L2 QD / SWE Own a production module One service or subsystem p99 latency, uptime, MTTR Production ownership across incidents L3 Senior Engineer Own a platform component Critical subsystem SLOs, design quality, mentoring Architecture impact beyond own team L4 Staff / Principal Engineer Set technical direction Multi-team platform Firm-wide standards, cost, reliability Technical strategy adopted firm-wide L5 Engineering Manager Lead a team 6–10 engineers Delivery, retention, quality Team performs without you L6 Head of Engineering / Technology Own the engineering function All engineering teams Tech roadmap, platform competitiveness Function is a competitive advantage L7 Deputy CTO / SVP Engineering Firm-wide architecture Security, hardware, infrastructure Multi-year architecture, risk posture C-suite readiness L8 CTO Technology as a firm pillar Firm strategy with peers Firm-level tech edge — Journey narrative. Years 0–2 (L0–L1): learn to write code that other people can trust. Tests, reviews, observability, on-call. Understand the trading domain enough to ask better questions.

search.title: Technology track (QD / low-latency / FPGA / infra / SRE / security)
search.text: Years 2–4 (L2): own a production module. Feel the pain of p99 latency and 3 a.m. incidents. Learn to debug under pressure. Years 4–7 (L3): own a critical subsystem. Design for failure. Mentor. Learn to say "no" to features that add latency or operational risk. Years 7–10 (L4): set architecture. Choose build vs buy, co-location strategy, language/runtime, hardware roadmap. Your leverage is now standards and platform. Years 10+ (L5–L6): lead engineering. Balance delivery speed with reliability and security. Build a bench of L4s. Branches: low-latency/HFT, FPGA/hardware, infrastructure/SRE, security, data platform, application/platform engineering, build/release. Lateral moves: tech → research engineering, tech → product, tech → ops (connectivity), tech → CTO track. Failure modes: over-engineering; hero-driven operations; ignoring p99/jitter; security debt; refusing to document; optimizing for elegance over trading outcomes. Promotion evidence (L2→L3): owned a critical subsystem through at least one major incident; measurable SLO improvement; design review leadership; mentorship; cross-team adoption of a tool or standard.

search.title: Data & ML Engineering track
search.text: Data & ML Engineering track Entry points: CS/statistics/engineering degrees; data platform engineering at scale-ups; ML infrastructure; database internals; lateral hires from big tech, exchanges, or other funds. The distinguishing test is not "can you use Spark" but "can you make 50 TB of tick data queryable, correct, and cheap at 3 a.m.

search.title: Data & ML Engineering track
search.text: before the open." Band Title Mission Scope Primary KPIs Promotion gate --- --- --- --- --- --- L0 Data / ML Intern Learn data discipline One pipeline or notebook Reproducibility, correctness Return offer L1 Data Analyst / Junior DE Deliver clean datasets One pipeline, one dataset Freshness, test coverage, documentation Independent pipeline ownership L2 Data Engineer / MLE Own a data domain Tick store, feature store, or model service SLA adherence, cost per TB, model latency Production ownership through a failure L3 Senior DE / Senior MLE Own the data platform or ML platform Multi-dataset platform, training infra Platform SLOs, adoption, lineage coverage Platform used by multiple desks L4 Staff DE / Principal MLE Set data/ML architecture Firm-wide platform and standards Cost, reliability, time-to-feature Architecture adopted firm-wide L5 Data/ML Engineering Manager Lead a platform team 6–10 engineers Delivery, reliability, talent Team performs without you L6 Head of Data / Head of ML Own the data function All data engineering, governance Data trust, regulatory readiness Function is a competitive advantage L7 Deputy CDO / SVP Data Firm-wide data strategy Governance, lineage, external data Data as an asset; audit-clean C-suite readiness L8 CDO / Chief Data Officer Data as a firm pillar Firm strategy with peers Firm-level data edge — Journey narrative.

search.title: Data & ML Engineering track
search.text: Years 0–2 (L0–L1): learn that data work is 80% correctness and 20% cleverness. Build pipelines with tests, idempotency, and backfills. Learn the difference between "the job ran" and "the data is right." Years 2–4 (L2): own a data domain — tick data, corporate actions, reference data, or a feature store. Feel the pain of a silent schema change and a stale partition on a live trading day. Build monitoring that catches it before the desk does. Years 4–7 (L3): own the platform. Design for cost, latency, and lineage. Learn that the hardest problem is not storage but semantics: two desks computing "volume" differently is a data incident waiting to happen. Years 7–10 (L4): set architecture. Lakehouse vs warehouse, batch vs streaming, build vs buy. Your job is to reduce the time from "researcher has an idea" to "researcher has clean data" from weeks to hours. Years 10+ (L5–L6): lead the function. Data governance, vendor licensing, regulatory data requests, and the political work of getting desks to adopt standards. Branches: market data engineering, tick/order-book storage, feature platforms, MLOps/model serving, data governance & lineage, alternative-data ingestion. Lateral moves: data → research engineering; data → quant research (strong candidates with statistics); data → technology platform; data → risk data/regulatory reporting.

search.title: Data & ML Engineering track
search.text: Failure modes: pipelines without tests; silent schema drift; "the data is always right" assumptions; building a platform nobody uses; hoarding data access instead of governing it; confusing tool adoption with data quality. Promotion evidence (L2→L3): platform or domain owned through at least one production data incident; measurable freshness/quality improvement; lineage and documentation adopted by others; a research team that ships faster because of your work.

search.title: Risk & Model Validation track
search.text: Risk & Model Validation track Entry points: quantitative finance, statistics, physics, engineering; bank risk/validation teams; model risk management; trading desk lateral moves (with independence guardrails). Risk is a second line function: it must be credible to the desk without being captured by it.

search.title: Risk & Model Validation track
search.text: Band Title Mission Scope Primary KPIs Promotion gate --- --- --- --- --- --- L0 Risk Intern Learn the risk framework One report or stress test Accuracy, clarity Return offer L1 Risk Analyst Monitor and report Daily exposure, limit reports Timeliness, zero missed breaches Independent coverage of a risk type L2 Risk Manager / Risk Engineer Own a risk domain Market, credit, or liquidity risk Limit breaches caught pre-trade, stress quality Domain owned through a stress event L3 Senior Risk Manager Own the risk framework for a desk cluster Multi-desk limits, scenarios Risk-adjusted returns, drawdown control Framework survives a crisis L4 Staff Risk / Lead Validator Set risk methodology VaR/ES, stress library, validation standards Model accuracy, regulatory acceptance Methodology adopted firm-wide L5 Risk Manager (people) / Head of Market Risk Lead a risk team 5–10 risk professionals Coverage, escalation quality Team credible without you L6 Head of Risk Own the risk function All risk types, limits, governance Firm risk appetite adherence CRO-ready; board trust L7 Deputy CRO / SVP Risk Firm-wide risk strategy Capital, liquidity, model risk Multi-year risk posture C-suite readiness L8 CRO Risk as a firm pillar Veto rights, firm strategy Firm survival and risk-adjusted growth — Model Validation sub-track (a specialization that can run L2–L7): Band Title Scope --- --- --- L2 Model Validation Analyst Validate one model family (pricing, risk, alpha) L3 Model Validation Quant Lead validation for a desk or model class; challenge assumptions L4 Lead Model Validator Own the validation standard, sampling, and revalidation cadence L5 Head of Model Risk Independent model risk function; report to CRO or board risk committee L6–L7 Head of Model Risk / Deputy CRO Firm-wide model risk governance, regulatory relationships Journey narrative.

search.title: Risk & Model Validation track
search.text: Years 0–2 (L0–L1): learn the numbers and the plumbing. Reconcile exposures, run the daily limit report, understand every field. The goal is to be the person who notices the number is wrong before the desk does. Years 2–4 (L2): own a risk domain. Build pre-trade checks, stress scenarios, and limit logic. Learn to say "no" early and explain why in the desk's language — P&L, not policy. Years 4–7 (L3): own the framework for a cluster of desks. Design limits that bind without strangling. Run stress tests that the desk respects because they reflect real tail behavior. Years 7–10 (L4–L5): set methodology and lead a team. Your credibility is your only currency; you cannot buy it with org charts. Build a validation function that finds real problems, not paperwork. Years 10+ (L6–L7): own the function. Advise the CEO on risk appetite, represent the firm to regulators, and hold the line when the desk is having its best month. Branches: market risk, credit/counterparty risk, liquidity/treasury risk, model validation, operational risk, regulatory capital, climate/emerging risk (rare in prop). Lateral moves: risk → research (model-building skills transfer); risk → compliance (regulatory overlap); risk → trading (desk experience, but requires cooling-off and independence rules); risk → treasury.

search.title: Risk & Model Validation track
search.text: Failure modes: becoming the desk's rubber stamp; reporting after the loss; VaR models that assume normality in a fat-tail market; validation that checks documentation instead of assumptions; escalation avoided to keep the peace. Promotion evidence (L2→L3): caught a material risk before it materialized; designed limits adopted by multiple desks; led a stress event post-mortem; independent validation memo that changed a model or a limit.

search.title: Compliance & Legal track
search.text: Compliance & Legal track Entry points: law degrees (JD/LLB), compliance/regulatory backgrounds from banks or exchanges, surveillance analysts, paralegals, regulatory affairs. In a <100-person firm this is often one combined function; at scale it splits into Compliance (CCO) and Legal (GC).

search.title: Compliance & Legal track
search.text: Band Title Mission Scope Primary KPIs Promotion gate --- --- --- --- --- --- L0 Compliance / Legal Intern Learn the rulebook One research task Accuracy, judgment Return offer L1 Compliance Analyst / Paralegal Execute compliance processes Filings, registrations, KYC On-time filings, zero misses Independent ownership of a process L2 Compliance Officer / Counsel Own a compliance domain Surveillance, reporting, licensing Clean exams, no findings Domain owned through a regulatory exam L3 Senior Compliance Officer / Senior Counsel Own the program for a business line Multi-jurisdiction, surveillance Regulatory relationships, zero enforcement Program survives an audit L4 Head of Compliance / Lead Counsel Set the compliance/legal program Firm-wide policies, training Regulatory standing Program is a competitive advantage L5 Compliance Director / Legal Director Lead a team 5–10 professionals Coverage, escalation Team credible without you L6 Head of Compliance / General Counsel Own the function All compliance or legal Board trust, regulatory standing C-suite readiness L7 Deputy CCO / Deputy GC Firm-wide regulatory strategy Multi-jurisdiction, M&A Regulatory strategy C-suite readiness L8 CCO / General Counsel Compliance/legal as a firm pillar Firm strategy, board Firm license to operate — Journey narrative.

search.title: Compliance & Legal track
search.text: Years 0–2 (L0–L1): learn the rulebook cold — exchange rules, market-abuse regulation, reporting deadlines, entity structures. Accuracy is the whole job. Years 2–4 (L2): own a domain: trade surveillance, regulatory reporting, licensing, or contracts. Build processes that survive an exam, not just a checklist. Years 4–7 (L3): own the program for a business line. Build relationships with regulators and exchanges. Learn to say "we can do this, but here's how" instead of "no." Years 7–10 (L4–L5): set the program and lead a team. Your job is to make compliance a design input, not a post-hoc review. Years 10+ (L6–L7): own the function. Advise the board, manage regulatory strategy across jurisdictions, and protect the firm's license to operate. Branches: trade surveillance, regulatory reporting (MiFID/EMIR/SEC/CFTC equivalents), exchange compliance, employment/comp legal, corporate/M&A, IP and data licensing, financial crime. Lateral moves: compliance → risk (overlapping control agendas); compliance → operations (regulatory ops); legal → corp dev; compliance → product (regulatory product design). Failure modes: checkbox compliance; being surprised by a rule change; saying "no" without alternatives; treating the regulator as an adversary; legal advice that ignores commercial reality.

search.title: Compliance & Legal track
search.text: Promotion evidence (L2→L3): owned a regulatory exam or audit with no material findings; built a surveillance or reporting process adopted firm-wide; advised on a new market/product launch end-to-end.

search.title: Finance & Treasury track
search.text: Finance & Treasury track Entry points: accounting (CPA/CA/ACCA), finance, economics; bank treasury/FP&A; audit; lateral hires from funds or brokers. Band Title Mission Scope Primary KPIs Promotion gate --- --- --- --- --- --- L0 Finance Intern Learn the books One reconciliation or report Accuracy, timeliness Return offer L1 Financial Analyst Produce reliable numbers Month-end, P&L attribution Close on time, zero restatements Independent ownership of a close L2 Senior Analyst / Controller Own a finance domain Accounting, tax, treasury ops Audit-clean books, cash accuracy Domain owned through an audit L3 Finance Manager / Treasury Manager Own the finance calendar Multi-entity close, treasury Cash efficiency, funding cost Framework survives a stress event L4 Head of Finance / Treasurer Set finance policy Capital, tax, audit, banking Capital efficiency, audit standing Policy adopted firm-wide L5 Finance Director Lead a team 5–10 professionals Delivery, controls Team performs without you L6 Head of Finance / CFO-1 Own the finance function All finance, treasury, tax Board-ready reporting CFO readiness L7 Deputy CFO / SVP Finance Firm-wide capital strategy Capital structure, M&A finance Capital plan C-suite readiness L8 CFO Finance as a firm pillar Firm strategy, capital, investors Firm capital efficiency — Journey narrative.

search.title: Finance & Treasury track
search.text: Years 0–2 (L0–L1): learn the close, the chart of accounts, and how P&L actually flows from trades to the general ledger. Accuracy and speed. Years 2–4 (L2): own a domain — accounting, tax, treasury operations, or FP&A. Build controls that scale. Learn that a reconciliation break is a risk signal, not an annoyance. Years 4–7 (L3): own the finance calendar. Multi-entity, multi-currency, multi-broker. Manage audits and banking relationships. Years 7–10 (L4–L5): set policy and lead. Capital allocation, transfer pricing, tax strategy, treasury risk. Your job is to fund the firm's edge at the lowest cost. Years 10+ (L6–L7): own the function. Board reporting, investor relations (with CEO), capital planning, and the trade-off between returning capital and reinvesting. Branches: accounting/control, treasury, tax, FP&A, capital planning, investor reporting, audit. Lateral moves: finance → risk (treasury/market risk overlap); finance → operations (settlements); finance → corp dev; finance → COO track. Failure modes: books that close late; reconciliation debt; treasury surprises on margin calls; tax positions that don't survive scrutiny; finance that reports history but never informs decisions. Promotion evidence (L2→L3): owned a clean audit; reduced close time or funding cost measurably; built a capital or treasury model used by the CEO.

search.title: Operations track
search.text: Operations track Entry points: finance/operations/business degrees; exchange or broker operations; trade support; military logistics; lateral hires from funds or prime brokers. Operations is the firm's immune system: it is invisible when healthy and existential when not.

search.title: Operations track
search.text: Band Title Mission Scope Primary KPIs Promotion gate --- --- --- --- --- --- L0 Operations Intern Learn the trade lifecycle One process Accuracy, speed Return offer L1 Operations Analyst Execute daily operations Reconciliations, settlements, connectivity Zero breaks unresolved overnight Independent process ownership L2 Trading / Market Ops Specialist Own an operational domain Exchange connectivity, corporate actions Uptime, break rate, incident MTTR Domain owned through an incident L3 Senior Ops Manager Own the ops calendar Multi-venue, multi-product Operational reliability Framework survives a market event L4 Head of Operations Set ops policy All trade ops, vendor management Cost, reliability, scalability Policy adopted firm-wide L5 Operations Director Lead a team 6–10 professionals Delivery, coverage Team performs without you L6 Head of Operations (COO-1) Own the operations function All ops, exchange relationships Operational resilience COO readiness L7 Deputy COO / SVP Operations Firm-wide operational strategy Multi-office, 24/6 coverage Scalability C-suite readiness L8 COO Operations as a firm pillar Firm strategy, execution Firm operational edge — Journey narrative. Years 0–2 (L0–L1): learn the trade lifecycle end to end — order, fill, allocation, settlement, reconciliation, corporate action. Be the person who catches the break. Years 2–4 (L2): own a domain.

search.title: Operations track
search.text: Exchange connectivity certifications, market-data entitlements, corporate actions, or clearing. Build runbooks. Automate the boring parts. Years 4–7 (L3): own the ops calendar. Coordinate across venues and time zones. Run incident response without drama. Years 7–10 (L4–L5): set policy and lead. Vendor management, exchange relationships, cost control, and the operational side of new market entry. Years 10+ (L6–L7): own the function. Operational resilience, business continuity, multi-office coverage, and the COO agenda. Branches: trade support, market ops/connectivity, settlements & clearing, corporate actions, vendor management, business continuity, regulatory operations. Lateral moves: ops → risk (operational risk); ops → compliance (regulatory ops); ops → technology (production support); ops → trading (market mechanics expertise). Failure modes: single-person processes; manual workarounds that become permanent; reconciliation debt; poor incident communication; treating ops as a cost center rather than a control. Promotion evidence (L2→L3): owned a market event or exchange outage response; reduced break rate or MTTR measurably; automated a process that removed a key-person risk.

search.title: Product & Business track
search.text: Product & Business track Entry points: product management, consulting, banking/BD, exchange or vendor roles, internal transfers from trading or technology. This track is optional below ~150 people; it becomes essential when the firm builds internal platforms or external partnerships.

search.title: Product & Business track
search.text: Band Title Mission Scope Primary KPIs Promotion gate --- --- --- --- --- --- L0 Product / BD Intern Learn the customer One research task Clarity, judgment Return offer L1 Product Analyst / BD Analyst Support discovery and deals One product area or deal pipeline Adoption, deal cycle time Independent ownership L2 Product Manager / BD Manager Own a product or partner One platform or partnership Usage, revenue/cost impact Shipped product or closed deal L3 Senior PM / Senior BD Own a portfolio Multiple products or partners Roadmap outcomes Portfolio impact L4 Head of Product / Head of BD Set the product/BD agenda Function-wide Adoption, commercial terms Strategy adopted firm-wide L5 Product Director / BD Director Lead a team 5–10 professionals Delivery, partnerships Team performs without you L6 Head of Product / Head of Business Own the function All product or BD Firm-level commercial impact C-suite readiness L7 VP Product / VP Business Development Firm-wide strategy Multi-year roadmap Strategic partnerships C-suite readiness L8 CPO / CBO / CSO Product/business as a pillar Firm strategy Firm growth — Journey narrative. Years 0–2 (L0–L1): learn the internal customer. Sit with researchers and traders; understand what makes their day hard. For BD, learn the exchange and vendor landscape. Years 2–4 (L2): own a product or a partnership.

search.title: Product & Business track
search.text: Ship something used daily; close a deal that saves or earns real money. Years 4–7 (L3): own a portfolio. Prioritize ruthlessly. Build a roadmap that the desks trust. Years 7–10 (L4–L5): set the agenda and lead. Product strategy, build-vs-buy, commercial negotiations, partner management. Years 10+ (L6–L7): own the function. Represent the firm externally; shape the platform and partnership strategy. Branches: internal platform product, data product, execution product, exchange partnerships, investor relations, corporate development. Lateral moves: product → technology; BD → corp dev; product → COO office; BD → CEO office. Failure modes: building for imaginary users; roadmap theater; BD deals that create operational debt; product managers without decision rights; measuring activity instead of outcomes. Promotion evidence (L2→L3): shipped a product with measurable adoption; closed a partnership with measurable economics; built a prioritization process others follow.

search.title: The CEO
search.text: The CEO Mandate: own the firm's strategy, capital allocation, risk appetite, and the executive team. The CEO is the only person whose job is the whole firm — every other seat is a domain. Dimension What it means in practice --- --- Owns Firm strategy and business model; capital allocation across desks and businesses; risk appetite (with CRO); C-suite appointments (with board); external relationships (investors, regulators, key partners); culture and talent bar. Decides alone Capital reallocation between desks within board-approved envelope; new business entry/exit; executive hires; firm-wide priorities. Decides with board Annual budget and capital plan; M&A; new lines of business; CEO succession; compensation philosophy for partners. Cannot delegate Final risk/return trade-off; the firm's ethical tone; the decision to stop doing something. Horizon 1–5 years, with a quarterly operating cadence. KPIs Risk-adjusted firm P&L; capital efficiency (return on capital deployed); drawdown control; strategy diversification; talent retention at L4+; regulatory standing; board confidence. Time allocation (target) 30% strategy and capital; 25% talent and org; 20% external; 15% risk and operations; 10% firefighting. If firefighting exceeds 25%, the org is under-built. The CEO's four hard trade-offs: Concentration vs diversification.

search.title: The CEO
search.text: One great strategy beats five mediocre ones — until it decays. The CEO decides how much of the firm's capital can depend on a single edge. Speed vs control. Move fast in research, slow in production. The CEO sets which side of the firm gets which bias. Star vs system. Pay up for a star trader, or build a platform that makes good traders great? The answer changes with scale and strategy half-life. Reinvest vs distribute. In a prop firm, retained capital is the growth engine; in a fund, returning capital is a signal of discipline. The CEO owns this call with the CFO. Failure modes: becoming the Chief Trader again (and neglecting the org); running the firm by P&L alone; avoiding a necessary C-suite hire because "it's faster to do it myself"; letting the founder's risk appetite become the firm's unexamined risk appetite; delegating culture. When the CEO is also the founder: the transition from founder-operator to CEO is a distinct job change. Signals it is time: the CEO is the bottleneck on more than two functions; decisions wait for their calendar; the executive team cannot resolve conflicts without them; the board asks for a succession plan.

search.title: The functional C-suite
search.heading: CTO — Chief Technology Officer
search.text: --- --- Mandate Own the technology platform, architecture, and engineering organization. Make technology a source of trading edge rather than a constraint. Owns Platform architecture; latency and reliability SLOs; engineering org and standards; security posture (with CISO); build-vs-buy; co-location and hardware strategy; technology budget. Decision rights Architecture standards; technology vendor selection; engineering org design; production change policy; veto on changes that breach SLOs or security policy. KPIs p50/p99/p99.9 latency and jitter; uptime; incident MTTR; deployment frequency and change-failure rate; infrastructure cost per unit of throughput; engineering retention. First 90 days Map the critical path from market data to order; establish SLOs and error budgets; identify the top three reliability risks; decide the architecture review process; assess the bench. Failure modes Building for elegance instead of edge; under-investing in reliability during growth; letting desks build shadow platforms; hiring managers who cannot code-review; treating security as a compliance checkbox. When to create Immediately in any firm with live trading and >10 engineers. Before that, a Head of Engineering (L6) with CTO scope is enough.

search.title: The functional C-suite
search.heading: CRO — Chief Risk Officer
search.text: --- --- Mandate Own the firm's risk framework and hold the veto. Ensure the firm survives its worst day and that risk-taking is deliberate, measured, and within appetite. Owns Risk appetite framework; limits (pre-trade and post-trade); stress testing; model validation; liquidity and counterparty risk; risk reporting to CEO/board; regulatory risk where applicable. Decision rights Veto on strategy launches, limit increases, new products, and model deployment where risk is material. Independent reporting line to the board risk committee (or board, in a small firm). KPIs Limit breaches (target: zero unapproved); stress-loss coverage; drawdown vs appetite; time-to-detect risk anomalies; validation findings closed; regulatory findings. Independence requirements Cannot report to the Head of Trading; compensation not tied to desk P&L; direct board access; authority to escalate without CEO approval. First 90 days Inventory every limit and where it is enforced; find the limits that exist on paper but not in code; run a firm-wide stress test; establish the risk committee cadence; meet every desk head. Failure modes Becoming the desk's risk translator rather than its challenger; over-modeling and under-escalating; VaR worship; blocking everything and losing credibility; no board access. When to create As soon as the firm runs material capital across multiple strategies.

search.title: The functional C-suite
search.heading: CRO — Chief Risk Officer
search.text: In a <30-person firm, the CEO + a senior risk lead may suffice — but the independence principle still applies.

search.title: The functional C-suite
search.heading: CFO — Chief Financial Officer
search.text: --- --- Mandate Own the firm's capital, financial integrity, and treasury. Ensure the firm is funded, the books are right, and capital is allocated to its best use. Owns Accounting and controls; treasury and funding; capital planning; tax; FP&A and budgeting; investor/partner reporting; audit relationship; banking and prime-broker relationships. Decision rights Financial policy; banking and broker relationships; capital structure recommendations; spend approvals above delegated thresholds; sign-off on financial reporting. KPIs Close timeliness and accuracy; audit findings; funding cost; cash and collateral efficiency; capital utilization; forecast accuracy; tax compliance. First 90 days Verify the P&L attribution chain from trade to GL; map all bank/broker accounts and signatories; assess close process and controls; build a 13-week cash forecast; meet auditors and key bankers. Failure modes Being a scorekeeper rather than a capital allocator; late or restated books; treasury surprises; tax positions that don't survive scrutiny; no view on return on capital. When to create When capital, entities, or investor reporting become material — typically before 50 people if the firm trades its own capital at scale.

search.title: The functional C-suite
search.heading: COO — Chief Operating Officer
search.text: --- --- Mandate Own the firm's operating engine: trade operations, connectivity, settlements, vendor management, and cross-functional execution. Make the firm run reliably at scale. Owns Trade and market operations; exchange and vendor relationships (with BD); operational resilience and business continuity; middle-office processes; firm-wide program execution; sometimes technology operations. Decision rights Operational policy; vendor selection within budget; incident command; process design; service levels with the front office. KPIs Operational incidents and MTTR; reconciliation break rate and aging; settlement failures; exchange certification timeliness; vendor cost; business continuity test results. First 90 days Map the trade lifecycle and every handoff; identify single-person dependencies; run an incident post-mortem review; establish SLAs with trading and technology; audit exchange certifications. Failure modes Becoming a super-ops-manager instead of a function leader; tolerating manual workarounds; poor incident communication; letting vendor sprawl; no succession depth. When to create When operations exceeds ~10 people or spans multiple venues/time zones, or when the CEO is spending >15% of time on operational issues.

search.title: The functional C-suite
search.heading: CCO / General Counsel — Chief Compliance Officer and Legal
search.text: --- --- Mandate Protect the firm's license to operate. Own regulatory compliance, legal risk, surveillance, and the firm's relationships with regulators and exchanges. Owns Compliance program; trade surveillance; regulatory reporting; licensing and registrations; legal affairs (contracts, IP, employment, corporate); regulatory change management; training. Decision rights Veto on activities that breach regulation or exchange rules; sign-off on new products/markets from a regulatory perspective; selection of outside counsel; regulatory communication strategy. KPIs Regulatory exams and findings; filing timeliness; surveillance alert quality and closure; contract cycle time; legal spend; training completion. First 90 days Build a regulatory obligations register by entity and jurisdiction; audit filings and registrations; review surveillance coverage; inventory contracts and IP; meet key regulators/exchanges. Failure modes Checkbox compliance; being surprised by rule changes; legal advice disconnected from commercial reality; over-blocking and losing influence; no relationship with regulators. When to create Compliance is non-negotiable from day one, but the seat can be combined with risk in a small firm (as in the source chart). Split into CCO + GC at ~100–150 people or when multi-jurisdiction.

search.title: The functional C-suite
search.heading: CDO — Chief Data Officer
search.text: --- --- Mandate Make data a trusted, governed, and competitive asset. Own the data platform, data quality, lineage, and data strategy. Owns Data platform and architecture (with CTO); data governance and lineage; data quality SLAs; vendor data licensing (with legal); alternative-data strategy; regulatory data requests. Decision rights Data standards; vendor selection for data; access policy; data quality gates for production models. KPIs Data freshness and completeness; incident rate; lineage coverage; cost per TB; time-to-data for researchers; license compliance. First 90 days Inventory every data source and its owner; find the datasets used in production with no lineage; establish quality SLAs; review vendor contracts for usage restrictions; build the data catalog. Failure modes Building a catalog nobody uses; governance as gatekeeping; ignoring cost; letting each desk define its own semantics; no authority over data quality. When to create When data engineering exceeds ~10 people or data spend becomes material (>5% of opex). Before that, a Head of Data (L6) reports to the CTO.

search.title: The functional C-suite
search.heading: Chief Scientist / Head of Research
search.text: --- --- Mandate Own the firm's research agenda and scientific standards. Ensure the firm's edge is real, documented, and renewing. Owns Research strategy and portfolio; research methodology and review standards; the signal pipeline; research talent bar; academic and external research relationships; long-horizon bets. Decision rights Research priorities; publication and external collaboration; research platform requirements (with CTO); kill decisions on research programs. KPIs Net Sharpe of research-originated strategies; research-to-production conversion; signal decay management; replication rate; external reputation (papers, talks, hires). First 90 days Review every live strategy's research provenance; audit the backtest protocol for leakage and overfitting; establish the research review cadence; assess the pipeline's health; set the kill criteria. Failure modes Chasing novelty over compounding; protecting pet projects; publishing without IP protection; losing the best researchers to desks; research that never ships. When to create When research exceeds one team or when the firm's edge depends on multi-year research bets. In the source chart this is a Head of Research (L6/L7); it becomes a C-suite seat at scale.

search.title: The functional C-suite
search.heading: Chief Trading Officer / Head of Strategies
search.text: --- --- Mandate Own the firm's trading P&L, capital deployment across desks, and market strategy. Turn research into live, profitable, risk-controlled trading. Owns Desk structure and mandates; capital allocation across desks (within CEO/CRO envelope); strategy pipeline and launch/retire decisions; execution model; market entry/exit; trader talent. Decision rights Desk capital allocation within limits; strategy launch/retire recommendations; execution venue selection (with ops/tech); trader promotion recommendations. KPIs Firm trading P&L and Sharpe; capital efficiency per desk; drawdown; capacity utilization; strategy concentration; trader retention. First 90 days Build a desk-by-desk P&L attribution and capacity view; identify the top three concentration risks; review every strategy's kill criteria; set the launch/retire process; meet every trader. Failure modes Being the biggest trader rather than the allocator; letting desks hide losses; over-diversifying into mediocre strategies; failing to retire decaying edges; no succession bench. When to create When there is more than one desk or when the CEO can no longer personally allocate trading capital. In the source chart this is Head of Strategies (L6/L7).

search.title: Minimum-viable vs scaled C-suite
search.text: Minimum-viable vs scaled C-suite The right question is not "what does a bank have?" but "which decisions are currently unowned or badly owned?" Firm stage C-suite (minimum viable) Added when Notes --- --- --- --- <30 people CEO; CTO or Head of Engineering; Head of Risk; Head of Trading; Finance lead (may be fractional) — Titles can be Head-of; the decision rights matter more than the title. 30–100 (source chart) CEO; Head of Strategies; Head of Research; Head of Technology; Head of Risk & Compliance; Head of Operations (split from HR); Finance lead CDO when data >10 people; GC when multi-jurisdiction Several seats are player-coaches. 100–250 CEO; CTO; CRO; CFO; COO; CCO/GC; Head of Research; Head of Strategies CDO; CISO; Chief Scientist First true executive team; formal committees. 250–500 Full C-suite + Chief Scientist, CISO, CBO/CSO, regional heads Deputy C-suite (L7) layer Multi-office, multi-strat, formal governance. The "one seat, two mandates" test. Combining seats is fine when the mandates share a decision rhythm and neither requires independence. Good combinations: COO + Operations; CCO + GC; CDO + CTO (early). Bad combinations: CRO + Head of Trading (independence violated); CFO + COO (control vs execution conflict at scale); CCO + CRO (challenge functions need separate escalation).

search.title: Minimum-viable vs scaled C-suite
search.text: Signals a seat must be created now: A class of decisions is being made by the CEO by default, and the CEO is the bottleneck. Two functions are in chronic conflict with no neutral owner. A regulator, auditor, or investor is asking for a named accountable executive. The function's spend or headcount crosses ~10% of the firm. An external event (exam, breach, outage, large loss) exposed an unowned risk.

search.title: CEO succession and founder transitions
search.text: CEO succession and founder transitions Why it matters earlier than you think: in a prop firm, the founder often is the risk appetite, the key relationships, and the capital allocator. If the firm cannot describe what happens when they are unavailable for a quarter, it is not yet an institution. The succession ladder: Stage What exists What it proves --- --- --- 0 — Founder-dependent No named successor; CEO makes all material decisions Nothing 1 — Emergency cover A named interim CEO (often COO or CFO) with delegated authority for 90 days The firm can survive a short absence 2 — Bench One or two L7/L8 executives with P&L or function ownership and board exposure A credible internal candidate exists 3 — Planned transition Board-approved successor, 6–12 month handover, explicit decision-rights transfer The firm can change leaders without changing strategy 4 — Institutional CEO role documented, board evaluates CEO, succession reviewed annually The firm outlives any individual Founder transition playbook: Separate the roles. Founder ≠ CEO ≠ CIO. Write down which hat is being worn in which meeting. Transfer decision rights deliberately. Start with capital allocation to desks, then external relationships, then the executive team's operating rhythm. Keep the strategy veto longest. Build the executive team before you need it. A founder who is the only L8 cannot delegate L8 decisions.

search.title: CEO succession and founder transitions
search.text: Give the successor real authority. A COO with no budget and no firing authority is a chief of staff, not a successor. Use the board. Even a small firm benefits from 2–3 external directors who can evaluate the CEO and hold the succession conversation. Plan the founder's next act. Founders stay healthier and firms transition better when the founder has a defined post-CEO role (chair, CIO, venture, research). Succession anti-patterns: naming a successor with no decision rights; "co-CEO" arrangements without a tie-breaker; delaying because the founder is still the best trader; choosing a successor who mirrors the founder rather than complements them; no emergency plan at all.

search.title: Product & Business leadership
search.text: Product & Business leadership At <100 people, "product" is usually a senior engineer with a roadmap and "business development" is the CEO having dinner with an exchange. That works until the firm has multiple internal platforms and material vendor/partner economics. Then the function needs a leader — not to add process, but to own decisions nobody owns. The two halves of the function: Half Mandate Primary customer Success metric --- --- --- --- Internal product Make research, execution, data, and risk platforms usable and adopted Researchers, traders, engineers Adoption, time-to-data, desk satisfaction External business Own exchange/vendor economics, partnerships, and (where applicable) investor relationships CEO, CFO, exchanges, investors Commercial terms, deal value, partner reliability Head of Product / Chief Product Officer (L6–L8): Owns: platform roadmap, prioritization across desks, product discovery, adoption, internal SLAs. Decision rights: roadmap priority within capacity; product requirements; build-vs-buy recommendations (with CTO); user research. KPIs: weekly adoption, time-to-first-value for new researchers, desk NPS, roadmap delivery, support ticket volume. Failure mode: becoming a project manager for the CTO, or building for the loudest desk instead of the firm.

search.title: Product & Business leadership
search.text: Head of Business Development / CBO (L6–L8): Owns: exchange and vendor relationships, fee schedules, market-data licenses, strategic partnerships, new-market commercial terms. Decision rights: negotiation mandate within CFO-approved economics; vendor shortlist; partnership recommendations to CEO. KPIs: cost savings, revenue from partnerships, contract cycle time, vendor concentration, partner uptime. Failure mode: signing deals that create operational debt, or optimizing fees while ignoring reliability and support. Investor Relations (L5–L8, only if the firm manages external capital): Owns: LP relationships, fundraising materials, reporting, due diligence, and capital-raise execution. Works with: CEO (story), CFO (numbers), CCO/GC (disclosure and marketing rules). KPIs: capital raised, LP retention, reporting timeliness, diligence cycle time. Failure mode: promising operational capabilities the firm cannot deliver; treating IR as marketing rather than a fiduciary relationship. When to create the seat: when internal platforms have more than ~50 users, when vendor/data spend is material (>5% of opex), or when the CEO is the de facto BD lead on more than two relationships. Before that, a senior PM or a Chief of Staff can carry the work.

search.title: The executive team operating cadence
search.text: The executive team operating cadence The C-suite is a team, not a set of independent fiefdoms. Its operating rhythm determines whether the firm makes decisions in days or quarters. The cadence: Forum Frequency Duration Purpose Output --- --- --- --- --- Executive stand-up Weekly 60 min Cross-functional decisions, risks, and blockers Decision log; owners; dates Business review Monthly 3 hours P&L, risk, technology, people, and strategy dashboards Actions; capital/limit recommendations Quarterly offsite Quarterly 1–2 days Strategy, capital allocation, org review, one hard problem Strategy memo; capital plan; org decisions Annual planning Annual 2–3 days Budget, strategy, compensation philosophy, succession Annual plan; board pack Board meeting Quarterly Half day Governance, CEO evaluation, capital, audit, risk Board minutes; resolutions Incident review As needed 60 min SEV-1/2 post-mortems and systemic fixes Actions; policy changes The weekly executive meeting agenda (60 minutes, ruthlessly timed): Numbers (10 min): P&L, risk utilization, incidents, hiring, cash. One page, pre-read. Decisions (30 min): Items that need a cross-functional call. Each item: decision requested, options, recommendation, owner. Risks and blockers (15 min): What is off-track, what needs escalation, what is stuck. One strategic topic (5 min): A rotating deep-dive, not a status update.

search.title: The executive team operating cadence
search.text: The executive team contract (write it down and sign it): Disagree in the room, align outside it. No undermining a decision after it is made. Bring options, not just problems. Every escalation includes a recommendation. Own your domain, respect others'. Do not make decisions in another executive's domain without their agreement. Escalate early. A problem that surfaces in week three is a crisis; in week one it is a decision. Protect the CEO's time. Batch decisions; do not route everything through the CEO. Tell the truth about your function. Bad news travels fastest upward; good news can wait. Decision log (the single most useful governance artifact): Review the log at every quarterly offsite. Decisions that were never revisited are either working or forgotten — both are worth knowing. The CEO's executive team checklist: [ ] Every function has a named leader with clear decision rights. [ ] The team disagrees productively in the room. [ ] No decision is waiting on the CEO for more than one week. [ ] Each executive has a credible successor or a plan for one. [ ] The team reviews the same numbers, not competing versions. [ ] At least one hard trade-off is made explicitly each quarter.

search.title: Committees and their charters
search.text: Committees and their charters Committee Chair Members Cadence Decisions it owns Quorum --- --- --- --- --- --- Investment / Strategy Committee CEO or Head of Strategies CRO, Head of Research, CFO, desk heads Weekly (launch/retire), monthly (portfolio) Approve new strategies, capital reallocation, market entry/exit, retire decaying strategies CEO + CRO + Head of Strategies Risk Committee CRO CEO, Head of Strategies, CFO, Head of Research Weekly Limit framework, limit changes above desk authority, stress scenarios, risk appetite changes CRO + CEO (CRO veto stands) Capital Allocation Committee CEO CFO, CRO, Head of Strategies Monthly / quarterly Firm capital plan, desk budgets, reinvest vs distribute, funding structure CEO + CFO Model Risk / Validation Committee Head of Model Risk (or CRO) CRO, Head of Research, independent validators, CTO Monthly Model approval, validation findings, model retirement, assumption changes CRO + independent validator + research Technology Architecture Review CTO Head of Engineering, low-latency lead, SRE lead, security lead, research engineering Bi-weekly Architecture standards, build-vs-buy, major platform changes, security exceptions CTO + 2 senior engineers Incident / Crisis Committee COO (or CTO for tech incidents) CRO, CTO, Head of Trading, Compliance, Ops Ad hoc, activated by severity Incident command, market withdrawal, client/regulator communication, post-mortem sign-off Incident commander + CRO + affected function head Promotion & Calibration Committee CEO (or COO) Function heads, 1–2 senior ICs, skip-level manager Semi-annual Promotions L1–L5, calibration across tracks, comp bands, L6+ recommendations to CEO/board CEO + majority of function heads Compliance & Regulatory Committee CCO CEO, CRO, GC, Head of Trading, Ops Monthly Regulatory change response, surveillance findings, new-product compliance, training CCO + CEO Board (or Advisory Board) Chair CEO, investors/partners, independent directors Quarterly CEO evaluation, capital plan, M&A, audit, executive comp, succession Majority of directors Charter rules that keep committees useful: Every committee has a decision log.

search.title: Committees and their charters
search.text: What was decided, by whom, with what evidence, and when it will be revisited. No committee without a veto-holder. Consensus committees drift; someone must own the final call. Standing attendees ≠ members. Keep decision membership small (3–5). Sunset review annually. If a committee met 12 times and changed nothing, it is a status meeting — merge or kill it. Decisions are documented in one place. Not in email threads, not in chat.

search.title: RACI for the decisions that matter
search.text: RACI for the decisions that matter R = Responsible (does the work) · A = Accountable (owns the outcome, one per row) · C = Consulted · I = Informed Decision CEO Head of Strategies Head of Research CTO CRO CFO COO CCO/GC CDO --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- --- Launch a new strategy I A R C C I I C I Allocate capital to a desk A R I I C C I I I Change a firm risk limit I C I I A C I I I Approve a model for production I C R C A (validation) I I I C Deploy a production code change I I I A C I I I I Declare a trading incident I C I R C I A C I Withdraw from a market A R C C C C R C I Sign a new exchange/vendor contract I C I C C A R C C Hire above L4 A C C C I I I I I Promote to L5 A R R R C C R R R Approve annual budget A C C C C R C C C Enter a new jurisdiction A C I C C C C R I Change compensation philosophy A C C C I R C I I Respond to a regulatory exam I C C C C C C A C Retire a data vendor I I C C I C C C A How to use this table: if two people believe they are A on the same row, you have a governance defect. Resolve it before the decision, not during it. If a row has no A, the decision will drift to whoever is loudest.

search.title: Strategy lifecycle and capital allocation
search.text: Strategy lifecycle and capital allocation Every strategy moves through six gates. Each gate has an owner, evidence requirements, and a kill criterion.

search.title: Strategy lifecycle and capital allocation
search.text: Gate Name Owner Evidence required Kill / stop criteria --- --- --- --- --- G0 Idea registration Head of Research Hypothesis, data source, expected edge, capacity guess Duplicate of existing work; no plausible economic rationale G1 Research approval Head of Research Literature/mechanism review, data availability, cost model, rough backtest Data unavailable or unlicensed; edge < cost G2 Signal readiness Head of Research + CRO OOS results, leakage audit, capacity estimate, turnover, decay analysis, risk assumptions OOS collapses; capacity too small; unmodeled tail risk G3 Production readiness CTO + CRO Code review, latency budget, failover, monitoring, limit integration, runbook No failover; latency breach; unvalidated risk checks G4 Pilot allocation Head of Strategies Paper/live pilot results, slippage vs model, operational fit Slippage > model by threshold; ops burden too high G5 Scale allocation Investment Committee 3–6 months live attribution, capacity utilization, correlation to existing book Sharpe decay; correlation crowding; drawdown beyond plan G6 Retire / replace Investment Committee Decay analysis, capacity saturation, better use of capital Persistent negative alpha net of costs Capital allocation mechanics (relative, no absolute numbers): Base allocation — each desk receives a capital and risk budget at the start of the year, expressed as a share of firm capital and a share of firm risk appetite.

search.title: Strategy lifecycle and capital allocation
search.text: Performance tranche — a portion is reallocated quarterly based on risk-adjusted performance, not raw P&L. New-strategy tranche — a protected pool for G4/G5 pilots, so new ideas are not starved by incumbent desks. Drawdown trigger — if a desk breaches its drawdown threshold, allocation is frozen and reviewed by the Risk Committee within one business day. Concentration cap — no single strategy may exceed a defined share of firm risk (e.g., 25–35%); no single venue or counterparty beyond a counterparty limit. Return of capital — if the firm cannot deploy capital at its hurdle rate, the CFO and CEO decide whether to distribute rather than dilute returns. The allocation conversation (quarterly, 60 minutes per desk): What did you earn per unit of risk? What capacity did you use? What is decaying? What would you do with 2× capital? What would you kill? The output is a decision, not a scorecard.

search.title: Risk limits, model risk, and incidents
search.heading: The limit hierarchy
search.text: Tier Limit type Set by Enforced by Breach handling --- --- --- --- --- T1 — Firm Capital at risk, max drawdown, gross/net exposure, liquidity Board / CEO + CRO CRO, pre-trade Immediate de-risking; board notification T2 — Desk Position, sector, factor, venue, counterparty CRO with Head of Strategies Risk system, pre-trade Auto-block or reduce; desk head notified T3 — Strategy Notional, order size, participation rate, inventory Desk head with CRO approval Trading system Auto-reject; trader review T4 — Operational Order rate, message rate, credit with broker, margin buffer CTO + CRO + CFO Infrastructure Throttle; incident Limit design principles: every limit has an owner, a rationale, a pre-trade enforcement point, an alert threshold (e.g., 80%), and a documented escalation. A limit that exists only in a spreadsheet is not a limit. Limit change process: request → risk impact analysis → CRO approval (T1/T2) or desk head + CRO notification (T3) → system update → post-change verification. Emergency increases require CRO + CEO, are time-boxed, and are reviewed at the next Risk Committee.

search.title: Risk limits, model risk, and incidents
search.heading: Model risk management
search.text: Element Requirement --- --- Inventory Every model used in trading, risk, or valuation is registered with an owner, version, and purpose. Tiering Tier 1 (material P&L/risk impact), Tier 2 (moderate), Tier 3 (limited). Tier 1 requires independent validation before production. Validation Conceptual soundness, data integrity, calibration, backtesting, sensitivity, stress, and limitations. Findings are graded and tracked to closure. Ongoing monitoring Performance vs expectations, drift detection, revalidation triggers (regime change, model change, material loss). Governance Model Risk Committee approves Tier 1 models; CRO owns the framework; validators are independent of model owners. Documentation Assumptions, limitations, failure modes, and the conditions under which the model should not be used.

search.title: Risk limits, model risk, and incidents
search.heading: Incident severity and response
search.text: Severity Definition Response Commander Communication --- --- --- --- --- SEV-1 Trading halted, material loss risk, data corruption, security breach, regulatory event Immediate; all hands; market withdrawal if needed COO or CTO CEO + CRO + board within 1 hour SEV-2 Degraded trading, partial outage, risk limit breach, failed settlement <15 min response Function head CEO + CRO same day SEV-3 Minor degradation, single strategy impact, non-critical data delay <1 hour Team lead Function head daily SEV-4 Cosmetic or no customer impact Next business day Owner Team Every SEV-1/2 gets a blameless post-mortem within 5 business days: timeline, impact, root cause, detection gap, response gap, and actions with owners and dates. The post-mortem is reviewed by the Incident Committee; repeat causes escalate to the CEO.

search.title: Separation of duties
search.text: Separation of duties The core control principle: no single person should be able to create, approve, execute, and reconcile the same transaction or risk. Activity Proposes Approves Executes Reconciles / validates --- --- --- --- --- New strategy Research Investment Committee Trading + Tech Risk + Finance Model in production Research Model Risk Committee Tech Independent validation Risk limit change Desk / Risk CRO Risk engineering Risk reporting New exchange/vendor Ops / BD CFO (contract), CTO (tech) Ops Finance Trade settlement Trading Ops Custodian/broker Finance reconciliation Compensation change Manager Calibration Committee CFO/CEO Board (L8+) Access to production Engineer CTO delegate SRE Security audit New market entry Strategy/BD CEO + CCO Ops + Tech Compliance review Where small firms must compromise (and how to do it safely): One person, two roles. Allowed only with compensating controls: peer review, automated reconciliation, audit logs, and a named independent reviewer outside the reporting line. CEO as final approver on everything. Acceptable below ~30 people; must be documented and revisited at every scaling stage. No separate model validation team. Use an independent senior quant (not the model owner) plus external review for Tier 1 models. Combined CRO/CCO.

search.title: Separation of duties
search.text: Acceptable in a small firm if the board (or an independent director) receives risk and compliance reports directly.

search.title: Performance philosophy by track
search.text: Performance philosophy by track Three rules that apply everywhere: Measure outcomes, not activity. Hours, lines of code, and number of reports are not performance. Risk-adjust everything. P&L without risk is not performance; latency without reliability is not performance; a clean audit is not performance if the firm lost money because risk said no to everything. Separate the scorecard from the story. The numbers inform the conversation; they do not replace it. A trader who made money by accident should not be paid like one who made it by design.

search.title: Performance philosophy by track
search.text: Track Primary metric Secondary metrics Quality / risk guardrails Anti-gaming rule --- --- --- --- --- Research Net Sharpe of research-originated strategies Research-to-production conversion; signal decay; capacity Leakage audit pass; documentation; OOS discipline No credit for backtest-only results; no credit for ideas that never ship Trading Risk-adjusted P&L (Sharpe/Sortino) Capacity utilization; fill quality; drawdown Zero unapproved limit breaches; kill-switch discipline No credit for P&L from limit breaches; drawdown-adjusted, not raw Technology SLO attainment (latency, uptime) Incident MTTR; change-failure rate; deployment frequency Security findings; on-call health; post-mortem closure No credit for heroics that mask systemic fragility Data / ML Data quality and freshness SLAs Platform adoption; time-to-data; cost per TB Lineage coverage; license compliance No credit for datasets nobody uses Risk Limit breaches prevented; risk coverage Stress-test quality; validation findings; time-to-detect Independence; escalation record No credit for blocking volume; no penalty for saying no with evidence Compliance / Legal Regulatory standing; zero enforcement Filing timeliness; exam findings; contract cycle time Independence; training completion No credit for "no findings" if the program is a checkbox Finance / Treasury Close accuracy and timeliness Funding cost; capital efficiency; forecast accuracy Audit findings; control gaps No credit for earnings management or delayed recognition Operations Operational reliability; break rate MTTR; settlement success; certification timeliness Incident communication; BCP test results No credit for firefighting that hides root causes Product / Business Adoption; commercial impact Roadmap delivery; partner satisfaction Desk trust; operational debt No credit for launches with no usage The 70/20/10 rule for evaluation input: 70% outcomes (the metrics above), 20% peer and stakeholder feedback (desk heads, risk, tech partners), 10% values and conduct (how the person achieves results).

search.title: Performance philosophy by track
search.text: A person who hits 100% of numbers but is corrosive fails the evaluation.

search.title: The promotion process and calibration committee
search.text: The promotion process and calibration committee Cadence: two cycles per year (spring and autumn). Off-cycle promotions only for exceptional scope changes (e.g., a desk head leaves and someone must step up) and require CEO + committee ratification. The seven-step process: Step Owner Artifact Time --- --- --- --- 1. Nomination Manager One-page nomination: current band, proposed band, scope change, evidence summary Week 1 2. Evidence pack Nominee + manager Promotion packet (Appendix C): scope, impact, evidence, peer feedback, development areas Weeks 1–2 3. Sponsor review Skip-level or senior IC Written sponsor statement: "I have seen this person operate at the next level" Week 3 4. Peer / stakeholder input 3–5 named reviewers Structured feedback: would you trust this person at the next band? Week 3 5. Calibration Committee Cross-track comparison; consistency check; decision (promote / defer / develop) Week 4 6. Decision communication Manager + committee chair Written outcome, rationale, and (if deferred) specific gaps and timeline Week 5 7. Compensation adjustment CFO + committee New band comp; effective date; communication Week 6 Calibration committee composition: CEO (chair), COO or function heads, one or two senior ICs from a different track (to prevent track-specific inflation), and a notetaker.

search.title: The promotion process and calibration committee
search.text: The committee must see all candidates at a band before deciding any, so that "L3 at desk A" means the same as "L3 at desk B." Calibration questions (the same for every candidate): What is the scope change? (If none, it is a comp discussion, not a promotion.) What evidence proves the person already operates at the next band — not that they might someday? Who depends on them at the next level? (Peers, juniors, the firm.) What would break if they left tomorrow? (If nothing, the scope may be smaller than claimed.) Would we hire this person at the proposed band from outside? (The external-market test.) What is the risk of promoting too early? (Peter Principle, title inflation, peer resentment.) Decision rules: Promote: evidence is sufficient, scope already exists or is funded, sponsor and peers agree. Defer with a plan: evidence is close but one gap remains; written 6-month development plan with named evidence required. Not yet: scope does not exist at the next band; the person is strong at current band. This is not a failure — say so explicitly. No "promotion by attrition." A person does not get a band because they are the last one standing. Appeals: a nominee may request one calibration review with new evidence. The committee's decision is final for the cycle; the appeal is heard by the CEO plus one independent function head.

search.title: The IC vs management dual track
search.text: The IC vs management dual track The fork at L4: up to L3, everyone is an individual contributor.
