At L4, two legitimate paths open: IC track (Staff / Principal) Management track (Manager / Head of Desk) --- --- --- Scope Technical or research domain across teams A team and a P&L or function Leverage Architecture, methodology, standards People, prioritization, capital allocation Success looks like The platform or research standard is better because you exist The team performs without you in the room Core skills Deep expertise, design judgment, teaching Hiring, coaching, prioritization, conflict, capital allocation Comp Comparable to management at the same band; may exceed at L5+ for exceptional ICs Comparable; upside through desk P&L share Prestige Must be equal. "Staff" is not a consolation prize. Must be equal. Management is not the only way to matter. How to try management without betting your career: Acting lead for 3–6 months — cover a manager's leave, lead a project team, run a hiring loop. Player-coach at L4 — lead 2–3 people while keeping technical work. Explicit return path — if management is not for you, return to the IC track at the same band within 12 months, no stigma, no comp loss. Manager training — before or immediately after the first direct report: hiring, feedback, performance conversations, legal basics (with GC), calibration.

search.title: The IC vs management dual track
search.text: Signals you should stay IC: you enjoy the craft more than the coordination; you resent meetings that are not technical; you would rather debug a latency regression than a conflict; your best days are deep-work days. Signals you should try management: you are already doing the coordination unofficially; you enjoy growing people; you can hold a standard without needing to be liked; you can make decisions with incomplete information and own the outcome. Signals you should return to IC: you are managing by spreadsheet; your team's technical quality is declining; you dread 1:1s; you are doing your old job at night and managing badly during the day. Return is a sign of self-awareness, not failure.

search.title: Compensation architecture (relative structure)
search.text: Compensation architecture (relative structure) Design principles: Pay for scope and impact, not title. The band sets the range; the contribution sets the position in the range. Risk-adjust variable pay. PnL share is calculated on risk-adjusted, cost-adjusted, and (where relevant) drawdown-adjusted P&L. Defer a meaningful share above L4. Deferral aligns time horizons and protects the firm against blow-ups. No pay for luck. A trader in a beta-driven year should not be paid like an alpha generator. Use peer-relative and risk-adjusted measures. Transparency in structure, confidentiality in amounts. Everyone should know how comp works; individual numbers stay private.

search.title: Compensation architecture (relative structure)
search.heading: Base compensation index (L1 = 1.00)
search.text: Band Base index Bonus target (% of base) Long-term incentive Total comp multiple of L1 (midpoint) --- --- --- --- --- L0 0.35–0.45 (stipend, annualized) — — 0.35–0.45 L1 1.00 20–40% — 1.2–1.4 L2 1.25–1.45 30–60% — 1.6–2.3 L3 1.6–1.9 50–100% — 2.4–3.8 L4 2.1–2.6 60–120% 0–10% of total 3.4–5.7 L5 2.7–3.3 80–150% 10–20% 5.0–8.3 L6 3.5–4.3 100–200% 20–30% 7.0–12.9 L7 4.3–5.3 120–250% 30–40% 9.5–18.6 L8 5.0–6.5 150–300% 40–60% 13–26 L9 6.0–8.0 200–400% 50–70% 18–40 How to read this table: it is a structure, not a salary survey. A firm can anchor L1 base anywhere; the ratios between bands should hold. The total comp multiple shows how steep the ladder is: at L8, total comp is roughly 13–26× L1, which is typical for a firm where the C-suite carries firm-level risk.

search.title: Compensation architecture (relative structure)
search.heading: Track modifiers
search.text: Track Base vs firm median Variable share Notes --- --- --- --- Research 1.0–1.1× Medium Paid for strategy impact, not just papers; research bonus pool tied to strategy P&L Trading 0.9–1.0× High Largest upside and downside; PnL share with high-water mark and deferral Technology 1.0–1.1× Medium Compete with big tech; equity/LTIP for L5+; on-call premium Data / ML 1.0–1.05× Medium Market-sensitive; compete with platform companies Risk 1.0× Low–medium Independence requires not tying pay to desk P&L Compliance / Legal 1.0× Low Market-based; no P&L linkage Finance / Treasury 1.0× Low–medium Firm performance pool, not desk P&L Operations 0.85–0.95× Low Reliability premium; shift/on-call allowances Product / Business 0.95–1.05× Medium BD commissions or deal-linked bonus where appropriate

search.title: Compensation architecture (relative structure)
search.heading: PnL share mechanics (trading and research)
search.text: A defensible PnL share formula has five components: Component Design choice Why --- --- --- Share % 5–20% of desk PnL above hurdle, varying by band and capital intensity Rewards value creation without transferring the firm's capital returns Hurdle Risk-free + capital charge (e.g., cost of capital) Ensures the firm earns its cost of capital before sharing Costs Execution, financing, data, infrastructure allocation Prevents "profitable" strategies that consume the firm's resources Risk adjustment Sharpe/Sortino scaling, drawdown penalty, tail-risk charge Prevents selling tail risk for steady carry High-water mark Losses must be recovered before new bonuses accrue Prevents "double-dipping" after a drawdown Deferral 30–50% above a threshold, vesting 3–4 years, forfeiture on breach Aligns with strategy half-life and misconduct risk Worked example (relative units, not currency): Desk risk-adjusted PnL after costs: 100 units Hurdle: 20 units → shareable pool base = 80 units Desk share: 12% → pool = 9.6 units Trader weight (based on attributed PnL and risk): 30% → 2.88 units Deferral: 40% → 1.15 units deferred, 1.73 units paid current If the desk had a prior loss of 10 units, the high-water mark reduces the base to 70 units before sharing.

search.title: Compensation architecture (relative structure)
search.heading: PnL share mechanics (trading and research)
search.text: Research PnL share follows the same logic but attributes PnL to the strategies that originated from the researcher's signals, net of the desk's execution and risk costs. Attribution rules must be written down before the year starts, not negotiated after.

search.title: Compensation architecture (relative structure)
search.heading: Equity and long-term incentives
search.text: Instrument Who Purpose Typical vesting --- --- --- --- Phantom equity / profit share L5+ in a prop firm Long-term alignment without diluting ownership 4 years, 1-year cliff Restricted equity L6+ Ownership mentality; retention 4 years, annual vest LTIP / carry L7–L9 Firm-level value creation 4–5 years, performance conditions Retention pool Key L4+ ICs Protect against poaching during a drawdown 2–4 years, clawback on exit

search.title: Retention, deferrals, clawbacks, and garden leave
search.text: Retention, deferrals, clawbacks, and garden leave Retention is a design problem, not a bonus problem. The best retention levers, in order: meaningful work, a manager who develops them, fair pay, and a firm that is winning. Cash retention bonuses are a last resort — they buy time, not loyalty. Mechanism When to use Design notes --- --- --- Deferred bonus L4+ with material variable comp 30–50% deferred; vesting 3–4 years; forfeiture on resignation or misconduct Clawback All variable comp above a threshold Triggers: restatement, risk-limit breach, misconduct, material model failure; look-back 2–3 years High-water mark Trading and research PnL share Prevents bonus accrual after losses; resets only when prior losses are recovered Garden leave Senior roles with access to strategy/IP Paid notice period; no work, no client contact; enforceability varies by jurisdiction — get legal advice Non-compete / non-solicit Key personnel Jurisdiction-dependent; must be reasonable in scope, duration, geography; do not rely on it as the only protection Notice period L4+ 3–6 months for desk heads and above; aligned with garden leave Succession depth Every L5+ role No single point of failure; documented handover The retention conversation (twice a year, separate from comp): ask what would make them stay, what would make them leave, and what they want to be doing in three years. Record it. Act on it.

search.title: Retention, deferrals, clawbacks, and garden leave
search.text: A counter-offer after resignation is usually too late. When a star threatens to leave: do not match blindly. Ask: is the threat credible? Is the person's edge portable or firm-dependent? What precedent does matching set? Would the firm be better off with a different allocation of that money? Sometimes the right answer is "we wish you well."

search.title: Underperformance and exits
search.text: Underperformance and exits Principle: underperformance is a management problem, not an HR problem. The manager owns the diagnosis, the plan, and the decision. HR-adjacent processes (documentation, legal review) are handled with the GC/COO, not an HR department. The performance spectrum: Category Definition Response Timeline --- --- --- --- High performer Consistently exceeds band expectations Stretch scope, promotion path, retention Ongoing Solid performer Meets expectations at band Development plan, next-band readiness Annual Developing Below band in one dimension, strong in others Targeted coaching, 90-day plan 90 days Underperforming Below band in core dimensions for 2+ cycles Formal improvement plan, explicit consequences 60–90 days Misconduct / risk breach Violation of policy, limits, or law Immediate investigation, possible termination Immediate The improvement plan (manager-owned): Diagnose specifically. "Your signals are not shipping" is not a diagnosis. "Three of four signals missed the G2 gate due to leakage" is. Define success in observable terms. What must be true in 60/90 days? Who verifies? Provide support. Training, mentoring, reduced scope, a different project. A plan without support is a paper trail, not a plan. Document. Written plan, signed by the employee, reviewed every two weeks. Decide. At the end: return to solid performance, extend once, or exit.

search.title: Underperformance and exits
search.text: Do not let a plan drift for a year. Exits with dignity: Be direct and early. The kindest exit is the one that does not surprise. Separate the person from the outcome. "This role at this band is not working" is different from "you are a failure." Protect the team. Communicate the change the same day, with a clear plan; do not let rumor fill the vacuum. Protect the firm. Access revocation, IP review, garden leave where appropriate, orderly handover. Pay fairly. Severance philosophy should be written down before it is needed; notice and statutory requirements vary by jurisdiction. Learn. Every involuntary exit gets a 30-minute review: was this a hiring error, an onboarding error, a management error, or a role-design error? The hardest case: a senior person who was once excellent. The firm's loyalty should be to the role, not the person's history. A desk head who can no longer allocate capital well is not helped by being left in the seat. Offer a dignified transition: IC track, advisory role, or a good exit.

search.title: Loop design by track
search.text: Loop design by track Universal structure: screen → technical depth → applied problem → collaboration/values → level calibration → decision. Total elapsed time: 2–3 weeks for L1–L2, 4–6 weeks for L3+, with a named recruiter-equivalent (a coordinator, not an HR department).

search.title: Loop design by track
search.heading: Research (QR / ML / alt-data)
search.text: Stage Format What it tests Pass signal Red flag --- --- --- --- --- Screen 30 min CV + research discussion Genuine research taste; clarity of past work Can explain why an idea worked, not just that it did Credits results to tools; cannot articulate mechanism Stats/probability 60 min Estimation, hypothesis testing, regression, causal inference Clean reasoning under uncertainty Memorized formulas; cannot derive Coding 60–90 min Python/pandas/numpy; reproducibility; data handling Correct, readable, tested code Copies from memory; ignores edge cases Research case Take-home or 3-hour live Hypothesis → data → test → conclusion Honest about limitations; checks leakage Overfits; hides negative results ML depth (if relevant) 60 min Model choice, regularization, validation, drift Knows when not to use ML Model zoo answers; no failure intuition Collaboration 45 min with 2 stakeholders Explains complex work to traders/engineers Adapts to audience; welcomes challenge Defensive; dismissive of non-researchers Level calibration Panel Scope, independence, judgment Operates at target band in the conversation Needs step-by-step direction at L3+

search.title: Loop design by track
search.heading: Trading (QT / execution / MM)
search.text: Stage Format What it tests Pass signal Red flag --- --- --- --- --- Screen 30 min Motivation, market intuition, risk temperament Clear interest in markets; calm Chasing glamour; reckless Mental math / probability 45 min Speed and accuracy under pressure Fast, correct, explains shortcuts Freezes; guesses without checking Market-making game 60 min Quoting, inventory, adverse selection Adjusts quotes to risk; manages inventory Quotes symmetrically; ignores flow Risk game / betting 45 min Position sizing, expected value, loss aversion Sizes by edge and bankroll Overbets; revenge-bets after losses Strategy discussion 60 min How they think about edge, decay, capacity Specific, testable hypotheses Vague "I'd use ML" answers Pressure / ambiguity 30 min Composure, honesty under uncertainty Says "I don't know" cleanly Bluffs; becomes defensive Level calibration Panel P&L ownership, drawdown history Owns outcomes; learns from losses Blames market, model, or colleagues

search.title: Loop design by track
search.heading: Technology (QD / low-latency / FPGA / infra / SRE / security)
search.text: Stage Format What it tests Pass signal Red flag --- --- --- --- --- Screen 30 min Systems background; trading interest Genuine curiosity about latency/reliability Only framework experience C++/Rust systems 90 min Memory model, concurrency, cache, allocators Reasons about hardware; writes correct lock-free code Avoids undefined behavior questions Latency design 60 min Tick-to-trade path, kernel bypass, batching End-to-end thinking; measures what matters Optimizes microbenchmarks only Debugging 60 min Live incident simulation; core dump; logs Systematic; forms hypotheses; verifies Random changes until it works Architecture 60 min Design a market-data or order-gateway system Trade-offs explicit; failure modes covered Over-engineers; ignores operability FPGA (if relevant) 90 min Verilog/VHDL, timing closure, pipelines Thinks in cycles and pipelines Synthesizes without timing analysis Collaboration / on-call 45 min Incident communication; post-mortems Blameless, specific, calm Blames others; hides mistakes

search.title: Loop design by track
search.heading: Data / ML Engineering
search.text: Stage Format What it tests Pass signal Red flag --- --- --- --- --- Screen 30 min Data platform background Has owned a pipeline in production Only notebook experience SQL / data modeling 60 min Joins, windows, schema design, partitioning Correct and efficient; thinks about scale Cannot reason about query plans Pipeline design 60 min Idempotency, backfills, schema evolution, SLAs Designs for failure and reprocessing Assumes data is always clean Coding 60 min Python/Scala/Java; testing Production-quality code Scripts without tests ML platform (if relevant) 60 min Training infra, feature stores, serving Understands train/serve skew Only model training Data governance 45 min Lineage, PII, licensing Treats data as a governed asset "Move fast, fix later"

search.title: Loop design by track
search.heading: Risk / Model Validation
search.text: Stage Format What it tests Pass signal Red flag --- --- --- --- --- Screen 30 min Risk framework experience; independence Clear on the second-line role Wants to be the desk's friend Derivatives / risk math 60 min Pricing, Greeks, VaR/ES, stress Derives and critiques models Formula recitation Model validation case 90 min Critique a model, find assumptions and failure modes Finds real weaknesses; prioritizes Nitpicks without judgment Limit design 60 min Design limits for a strategy Balances control and commerce Either blocks everything or nothing Regulatory / governance 45 min Framework, reporting, escalation Knows what "independent" means Treats compliance as paperwork Pressure / conflict 30 min Saying no to a senior trader Firm, evidence-based, calm Avoids conflict or escalates everything

search.title: Loop design by track
search.heading: Compliance / Legal
search.text: Stage Format What it tests Pass signal Red flag --- --- --- --- --- Screen 30 min Regulatory background; commercial sense Can explain a rule's purpose Rule recitation without judgment Technical 60 min Market-abuse rules, reporting, licensing Specific and current Outdated knowledge Scenario 60 min New market/product launch; identify obligations Structured, risk-based "We'll ask outside counsel" for everything Judgment 45 min Competing commercial and regulatory pressure Offers alternatives, not just "no" Rigid or captured Drafting (legal) 60 min Contract/policy drafting Clear, precise, commercial Boilerplate without thought

search.title: Loop design by track
search.heading: Finance / Treasury
search.text: Stage Format What it tests Pass signal Red flag --- --- --- --- --- Screen 30 min Accounting/tax/treasury background Owned a close or treasury function Only audit experience Accounting 60 min Revenue recognition, consolidation, controls Precise; knows GAAP/IFRS differences Hand-waves Treasury 60 min Cash forecasting, collateral, FX, funding Thinks in cash and risk Only reporting P&L attribution 60 min Trade → GL → attribution End-to-end understanding Cannot trace a trade Audit / controls 45 min Control design; audit management Practical, risk-based Checkbox mentality

search.title: Loop design by track
search.heading: Operations
search.text: Stage Format What it tests Pass signal Red flag --- --- --- --- --- Screen 30 min Trade lifecycle experience Owned a process end-to-end Only one narrow task Lifecycle 60 min Order → fill → allocation → settlement Complete picture Gaps at handoffs Incident 60 min Exchange outage / settlement fail simulation Calm, prioritized, communicative Panics or hides Reconciliation 45 min Find and resolve a break Systematic; root cause Plugs the number Exchange / vendor 45 min Connectivity, certifications, fees Commercial awareness Purely administrative

search.title: Loop design by track
search.heading: Product / Business
search.text: Stage Format What it tests Pass signal Red flag --- --- --- --- --- Screen 30 min Product/BD background in technical domains Shipped something used by experts Only consumer/product-marketing Discovery 60 min Interview a "desk head" (role-play) Asks good questions; finds the real problem Pitches immediately Prioritization 45 min Roadmap trade-offs with constraints Explicit criteria; says no Everything is P0 Commercial (BD) 60 min Negotiation case; unit economics Creates value, not just price Wins the deal, loses the relationship Execution 45 min Cross-functional delivery Owns outcomes; manages stakeholders Coordinates without authority

search.title: Entry points and level calibration
search.text: Entry points and level calibration Entry point Typical band What to test Common mistake --- --- --- --- Intern L0 Learning speed, reasoning, collaboration Testing knowledge instead of thinking New graduate L1 Fundamentals, coding, research potential Expecting production experience PhD / postdoc L1–L2 Research depth, coding, commercial instinct Overweighting publications Industry lateral (2–5 yrs) L2–L3 Ownership, scope, domain depth Mapping title instead of scope Senior lateral (5–10 yrs) L3–L4 Architecture/strategy ownership, mentorship Hiring for pedigree, not evidence Desk head / PM L5 P&L track record, capital allocation, team building Ignoring risk record and drawdowns C-suite L8 Firm-level judgment, board/regulator experience Hiring a brand name without domain fit Level calibration in the interview: the same candidate can be L2 or L3 depending on how they handle scope.

search.title: Entry points and level calibration
search.text: Test it explicitly: Question type L2 answer L3 answer L4 answer --- --- --- --- "Tell me about your last project." Describes their component Describes the strategy/system and its outcomes Describes the portfolio, trade-offs, and what they'd do differently at scale "How would you approach this problem?" Proposes a method Proposes a method, states assumptions, defines success Frames the problem, considers alternatives, identifies what would change their mind "Tell me about a failure." Describes a mistake Describes a systemic lesson and a change they made Describes an organizational failure and how they changed the system "How do you decide what to work on?" Waits for direction Prioritizes within a mandate Sets the mandate and defends the trade-off The "next-band" test: for a promotion or a senior hire, ask: "What would you do in your first 90 days that you could not do in your current role?" If the answer is "the same things, faster," the scope is not there.

search.title: Scorecards and the hiring bar
search.text: Scorecards and the hiring bar Scorecard dimensions (1–4 scale; 3 = meets the bar, 4 = exceptional): Dimension Weight (IC) Weight (manager) What a 3 looks like --- --- --- --- Technical depth 35% 25% Solves problems at the target band without help; explains trade-offs Problem framing 20% 20% Turns ambiguity into a testable plan; knows what would falsify it Execution / ownership 20% 20% Ships; handles setbacks; follows through Collaboration 15% 20% Raises the team's quality; gives and takes feedback Judgment / values 10% 15% Honest about uncertainty; puts firm before self; respects risk Decision rules: Hire: no dimension below 3, at least one 4, and unanimous interviewer support. Strong hire: multiple 4s, no concerns. No hire: any dimension at 1, or two at 2, or a material values concern. "Maybe" is a no. If the loop cannot articulate why the person will succeed at the target band, do not hire. No hiring to fill a seat. A vacant seat is cheaper than a wrong hire. No level inflation to close a candidate. If they are L2, hire them at L2 with a path; do not hire at L3 to win the offer. Interviewer calibration: every interviewer writes feedback before the debrief, independently. The debrief discusses evidence, not impressions. Track interviewer accuracy against 12-month performance; retrain or remove interviewers whose "strong hire" candidates underperform.

search.title: Scorecards and the hiring bar
search.text: The offer: Be transparent about the band and the path. Show the ladder; explain what L3 → L4 requires. Compete on the whole package: base, bonus structure, equity, learning, colleagues, and mission — not just cash. Do not over-promise. A promise about promotion or comp that the firm cannot keep becomes a retention problem in year two. Close with a named buddy and a 90-day plan (Appendix D). The onboarding experience starts before day one. Hiring anti-patterns: hiring in your own image; "brilliant jerk" exceptions; skipping the values interview for senior candidates; using the same loop for every level; letting the loudest interviewer decide; ghosting candidates; negotiating against yourself.

search.title: Current state (<100 people)
search.text: Current state (<100 people) Current state · <100 people. Notes on this chart: HR is removed. The source chart's "Head of HR & Operations" is split; Operations remains as its own pillar, and people processes are manager/CEO responsibilities (Part VII). Finance is often a lead or fractional CFO at this stage; it becomes a full pillar at scale. Data sits under Technology here; it becomes its own function (CDO) at 100–250. Compliance sits under Risk here; it splits into CCO/GC at 100–250. Dashed reporting (not shown) should connect the CRO to the board or an independent director to preserve veto independence.

search.title: Scale-up (100–250 people)
search.text: Scale-up (100–250 people) Scale-up · 100–250 people. What changed from <100: Every pillar now has a C-suite owner and an L6 layer beneath it. Trading has desk heads between the CTO/Head of Strategies and the pods. Research splits by research type, not by desk. Risk adds model validation and stress testing as independent functions. Compliance and Legal split from Risk. Data becomes its own function with governance.

search.title: Multi-pod / multi-office (250–500 people)
search.text: Multi-pod / multi-office (250–500 people) Multi-pod / multi-office · 250–500 people. What changed from 100–250: A Deputy layer (L7) appears under each C-suite officer — the bridge band. Trading becomes regional + global product lines (execution, market making). Risk splits credit/counterparty from market and liquidity risk. Legal separates from Compliance. Security becomes a CISO seat. Business becomes a CBO with product, BD, and corp dev.

search.title: Internal views: desk, research pod, platform
search.text: Internal views: desk, research pod, platform

search.title: Internal views: desk, research pod, platform
search.heading: A trading desk (2–5 pods)
search.text: A trading desk · 2–5 pods. Desk design rules: A pod has one P&L owner (PM) and a small team of 3–8. Embedded QR/QD sit with the desk but report through their functional ladder for calibration — dual accountability, single P&L owner. Desk risk is independent of the PM and reports to the CRO, even when physically seated with the desk. Span of control for a desk head: 3–5 pods, not 10.

search.title: Internal views: desk, research pod, platform
search.heading: A research pod
search.text: A research pod. Research pod design rules: Pods are organized by research question, not by asset class. Each pod has a named lead who owns the research agenda and the review. Research engineering is shared: backtesting, feature store, experiment tracking. Pod size: 3–6 researchers, so review is rigorous but not bureaucratic.

search.title: Internal views: desk, research pod, platform
search.heading: The platform view
search.text: Platform architecture. Platform design rules: One data plane. No desk builds its own tick store. One execution plane. No desk builds its own gateway. Control plane is independent. Risk checks cannot be bypassed by the execution path. Research and production share semantics. The same feature definitions are used in backtest and live.

search.title: When to add each C-suite role
search.text: When to add each C-suite role Role Trigger to create Cost of waiting too long Cost of hiring too early --- --- --- --- CTO >10 engineers, or technology is on the critical path of P&L Latency/reliability debt; desks build shadow platforms; outages A senior leader with no org to lead; disintermediates the Head of Engineering CRO Material capital across multiple strategies, or a near-miss Risk limits live in spreadsheets; a single desk can sink the firm A blocker with no mandate; desks route around them CFO Multiple entities, material capital, investor/partner reporting Late books, treasury surprises, tax exposure Expensive scorekeeper if the firm is still small COO Ops >10 people, multi-venue, or CEO spending >15% on operations Operational fragility; key-person risk; incident chaos Process bureaucracy before there is process to run CCO / GC Multi-jurisdiction, regulatory exams, or >100 people Regulatory surprise; license risk; contract exposure Legal overhead on a firm that has no legal complexity yet CDO Data team >10, data spend >5% of opex Data trust erodes; duplicate pipelines; lineage gaps A catalog nobody uses; governance before volume Chief Scientist Research >1 team, or multi-year research bets Research becomes desk-driven and short-term A figurehead without a research org CISO External-facing systems, regulated data, or >150 people Security incident; regulatory finding A security org with nothing to secure CBO / Head of Product Internal platforms used by >50 people, or external partnerships Platform sprawl; bad vendor deals Product process without users The "interim" pattern: before the full seat, appoint an acting or deputy at L7 with a written mandate and a 6-month review.

search.title: When to add each C-suite role
search.text: This tests the need and the person without creating a permanent layer prematurely. The "two hats" rule: if a C-suite officer wears two hats for more than 12 months, one of them is being done badly. Name which one, measure it, and set a date to split.

search.title: Business-model variants
search.text: Business-model variants The same ladder, different center of gravity.

search.title: Business-model variants
search.text: Dimension HFT / prop (source chart) Multi-strat fund Bank quant desk Crypto / digital assets --- --- --- --- --- Primary edge Latency, microstructure, execution Alpha breadth, risk allocation, talent Distribution, balance sheet, client flow Volatility, fragmentation, 24/7 markets Org center Technology + trading pods PMs + risk + capital allocation Desk + control functions Engineering + risk + compliance PM autonomy Desk head owns P&L; PMs within High — PMs are profit centers Low — desk head owns; traders execute Medium — pods with token/instrument mandates Risk function Pre-trade, latency-aware, independent Central, powerful, portfolio-level Strong control culture, model risk 24/7 monitoring, custody/counterparty risk Tech ratio 40–60% of headcount 20–35% 20–30% 40–60% Research model Shared research, desk-embedded Central research + PM-embedded Desk research + quant library Fast-cycle, on-chain data, open research Compliance weight Medium–high (exchange rules) High (investor, regulatory) Very high High and fast-changing Comp shape PnL share + equity PnL share (PM), carry Base-heavy, bonus pool PnL share + tokens/equity Key failure mode Latency/ops fragility; concentration PM blow-up; crowding Bureaucracy; slow decisions Custody, regulation, 24/7 burnout Ladder adaptation Standard L0–L9 Add PM track at L5–L7; CIO at L9 Map bank titles; add control layers Add custody/treasury ops; 24/7 shifts If you are a bank or multi-strat: keep the bands but expect the title translation to do more work.

search.title: Business-model variants
search.text: A bank "VP" is often L3–L4 in scope; a multi-strat "PM" is L5–L6 with P&L. Calibrate on decision rights, not titles. If you are crypto: add explicit custody, wallet security, and 24/7 incident responsibilities to Operations and Risk; the "market close" assumption in traditional ops does not exist. Compliance is a moving target — build a regulatory change process, not a static policy.

search.title: Multi-office, remote/hybrid, and regulatory notes
search.text: Multi-office, remote/hybrid, and regulatory notes

search.title: Multi-office, remote/hybrid, and regulatory notes
search.heading: Multi-office
search.text: Decision Guidance --- --- When to open a second office When a talent market is inaccessible remotely, a venue/regulator requires presence, or a time zone is strategically important (e.g., APAC coverage). What to centralize Risk limits, capital allocation, technology architecture, compliance policy, compensation philosophy. What to localize Hiring, desk operations, exchange relationships, local regulatory liaison. Reporting lines Functional reporting (research → Head of Research) beats geographic reporting for expertise; geographic heads own local operations and compliance. Risk Two offices can drift into two firms. Mitigate with shared systems, rotating leadership, and a single P&L attribution standard.

search.title: Multi-office, remote/hybrid, and regulatory notes
search.heading: Remote / hybrid
search.text: Role type Remote fit Notes --- --- --- Research High Deep work benefits; needs strong written culture and async review Technology High Distributed teams work if on-call and incident command are explicit Trading Low–medium Latency, market feel, and desk communication favor proximity; remote trading is possible but requires rigorous controls Risk / Compliance Medium Independent review can be remote; regulatory relationships often local Operations Low Hands-on exchange/vendor work and incident response favor on-site Leadership Medium Hybrid works if the executive team meets in person regularly Remote operating rules: written decisions, explicit handoffs, overlap hours for desks, no remote-only on-call without escalation paths, and a documented "what must be in person" list (incident command, hiring debriefs, strategy reviews, compensation conversations).

search.title: Multi-office, remote/hybrid, and regulatory notes
search.heading: Regulatory notes (non-exhaustive; get local counsel)
search.text: Licensing: proprietary trading vs managing external capital changes the regulatory perimeter entirely. A prop firm that takes outside capital becomes a fund/asset manager with different obligations. Market conduct: surveillance, best execution (where applicable), market-abuse monitoring, order-record retention. Reporting: transaction reporting, position limits, large-trader obligations, short-selling rules — jurisdiction-specific. Data licensing: exchange market-data agreements often restrict redistribution and non-display use; alternative-data licenses may restrict use for trading. Employment: non-competes and garden leave are jurisdiction-dependent; deferred comp and clawbacks need local advice. Cross-border: remote employees and contractors can create tax and regulatory presence in a jurisdiction. Crypto: custody, AML/KYC, travel rule, and exchange licensing vary widely and change quickly. The compliance scaling rule: compliance headcount should scale with jurisdictions × products × regulated entities, not with total headcount. A 300-person single-jurisdiction prop firm may need less compliance than a 120-person multi-jurisdiction fund.

search.title: Anti-patterns
search.text: Anti-patterns # Anti-pattern Symptom Root cause Fix --- --- --- --- --- 1 Title inflation Everyone is a VP; titles don't predict scope Retention via titles instead of comp/scope Enforce bands; audit titles annually 2 Player-coach trap Managers keep their old IC work and manage badly No explicit time allocation; no management training Define manager expectations; measure team outcomes 3 Shadow platforms Each desk has its own data store/gateway Central platform too slow or unresponsive Platform SLAs; chargeback; architecture review 4 Risk as rubber stamp Risk reports arrive after the loss CRO lacks independence or board access Independent reporting line; veto in writing 5 Research theater Many papers, few production strategies No G2/G3 gates; incentives reward novelty Research-to-production metric; kill criteria 6 Hero operations One person saves the day repeatedly No automation, no runbooks, no depth Document, automate, cross-train, measure MTTR 7 Promotion by attrition People promoted because they stayed longest Weak calibration; no external benchmark Evidence-based packets; external-market test 8 Consensus governance Committees meet, nothing is decided No veto-holder; unclear accountability Single A per decision; decision logs 9 Comp without risk adjustment Traders paid on raw P&L; tail risk accumulates Bonus formula ignores drawdown/costs Risk-adjusted pool; high-water mark; deferral 10 Hiring for pedigree Great CVs, weak ownership Interview tests credentials, not scope Level-calibrated loops; work samples 11 Founder bottleneck Every decision waits for the CEO No delegated authority; no L8 bench Decision-rights map; succession plan 12 Bureaucracy before scale Process for a 500-person firm at 60 people Copying a bank org chart Add process only when a bottleneck appears 13 Data sprawl Five versions of "volume"; no lineage No CDO/data governance Single data plane; ownership; lineage 14 Compliance as "no" Business avoids compliance until launch Compliance not in design; no alternatives Regulatory design review at G1 15 Star dependency One trader/researcher is the firm No documentation; no bench; no succession Knowledge capture; co-ownership; retention depth 16 Silent strategy decay Old strategies shrink but nobody retires them No decay monitoring; sunk-cost bias G6 retire gate; capital reallocation 17 Over-diversification Many mediocre strategies; no edge Fear of concentration; weak kill discipline Concentration limits with deliberate bets 18 Culture of blame Incidents produce blame, not fixes Leaders punish honesty Blameless post-mortems; reward detection 19 Compensation secrecy People don't know how comp works Fear of conflict Transparent structure, private amounts 20 Scale without standards Each new office/desk reinvents the firm No written operating model This document; onboarding; architecture review The meta-anti-pattern: copying another firm's org chart.

search.title: Anti-patterns
search.text: Your structure should follow your edge — if your edge is latency, technology and ops are central; if your edge is alpha breadth, research and risk allocation are central; if your edge is client flow, distribution and compliance are central. Structure follows strategy, not fashion.

search.title: Appendix A — One-page cheat sheet
search.text: Appendix A — One-page cheat sheet The ladder Band Title Owns Decides alone Comp shape --- --- --- --- --- L0 Intern A task Nothing Stipend L1 Analyst A component How, within bounds Base + small bonus L2 Quant/Trader/Engineer A signal/module/book slice Day-to-day execution Base + bonus L3 Senior A strategy/system/function Technical calls in domain + impact award L4 Staff/Principal/Desk Lead A platform or multi-strategy cluster Direction of the area + PnL share/equity L5 Manager/Head of Desk Desk P&L + team Capital within limits PnL share + equity L6 Director/Head of Function A function Function strategy/budget Profit pool + equity L7 VP/SVP/Deputy C-suite A firm-wide domain Policy within mandate Equity L8 C-suite A firm pillar Functional authority; veto where required Equity + LTIP L9 CEO The firm Final capital/strategy call Equity The tracks: Research · Trading · Technology · Data/ML · Risk & Validation · Compliance & Legal · Finance & Treasury · Operations · Product & Business. The governance non-negotiables Risk has a veto and independent board access. Every material decision has exactly one accountable owner. No strategy goes live without G2 (signal) and G3 (production) gates. Every model in production has an independent validation and a documented failure mode. Every SEV-1/2 incident gets a blameless post-mortem within 5 days.

search.title: Appendix A — One-page cheat sheet
search.text: No promotion without a written packet, a sponsor, and calibration. No single person can create, approve, execute, and reconcile the same trade. Compensation above L4 is deferred and risk-adjusted. The manager's monthly checklist [ ] One skip-level conversation per direct report's team [ ] Review desk/team P&L or SLOs with the team, not just the numbers [ ] Check open risk findings and incident actions [ ] Review hiring pipeline and at least one interview [ ] Identify one person ready for more scope and one at risk of stagnation [ ] Read one research memo or design doc end-to-end [ ] Ask: what decision is stuck, and who owns it? The CEO's quarterly checklist [ ] Capital allocation review by desk and strategy [ ] Risk appetite review with CRO [ ] Talent review: L5+ bench, succession, retention risks [ ] Technology and platform roadmap review with CTO [ ] Regulatory and compliance standing with CCO/GC [ ] Financial position and funding with CFO [ ] One external relationship deepened (investor, exchange, regulator, academic) [ ] One thing stopped (strategy, project, vendor, process)

search.title: Appendix B — Level & title glossary
search.text: Appendix B — Level & title glossary Term Meaning --- --- Band The firm-wide level (L0–L9) that standardizes scope, autonomy, and comp across tracks. Track A functional career path (research, trading, technology, etc.) with its own titles and competencies. Pod A small trading or research team (3–8 people) with a clear mandate and P&L or research ownership. Desk A group of 2–5 pods under a desk head, with an aggregate P&L and capital budget. PM (Portfolio Manager) The person accountable for a book or strategy pod's P&L and risk. QR / QT / QD Quantitative Researcher / Trader / Developer — the three core IC archetypes. IC track The individual-contributor path (Staff/Principal) that runs parallel to management. Dual track The principle that IC and management paths are equally prestigious and compensated. Calibration The cross-team process that ensures a band means the same thing everywhere. Span of control The number of direct reports; healthy range for a manager is 5–8, for a desk head 3–5 pods. RACI Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed — a decision-rights matrix. Alpha Excess return not explained by market exposure. Sharpe ratio Excess return divided by volatility; the core risk-adjusted performance measure. Sortino ratio Excess return divided by downside deviation; penalizes only downside volatility. Drawdown Peak-to-trough decline in P&L or NAV.

search.title: Appendix B — Level & title glossary
search.text: Capacity The amount of capital a strategy can deploy before returns degrade materially. Decay The erosion of a signal's predictive power over time or as more capital uses it. Turnover Trading volume relative to capital; drives costs and capacity. Slippage The difference between expected and realized execution price. Implementation shortfall Total cost of executing an order vs the decision price, including market impact and delay. VWAP / TWAP Volume- or time-weighted average price execution benchmarks. Queue position A trader's place in the limit order book; critical for fill probability. Adverse selection The risk that a counterparty trades against you precisely when you are wrong. Market making Quoting two-sided prices to earn the spread while managing inventory. Inventory risk The risk of holding a position while quoting or executing. Tick-to-trade latency Time from receiving a market-data tick to sending an order. Co-location Placing servers physically close to an exchange's matching engine to reduce latency. Kernel bypass Networking techniques (e.g., DPDK, Solarflare) that skip the OS network stack for lower latency. FPGA Field-programmable gate array; hardware used for ultra-low-latency market-data and order processing. OMS / EMS Order Management System / Execution Management System. VaR Value at Risk; a quantile loss estimate over a horizon and confidence level.

search.title: Appendix B — Level & title glossary
search.text: Expected Shortfall (ES) Average loss beyond the VaR threshold; more tail-sensitive than VaR. Stress test Scenario analysis of portfolio losses under extreme but plausible market moves. Model risk The risk of loss from incorrect or misused models. Model validation Independent review of a model's conceptual soundness, data, calibration, and limitations. Pre-trade risk Limits and checks applied before an order is sent to the market. Limit hierarchy Tiered risk limits (firm → desk → strategy → operational) with owners and enforcement points. Kill switch A control that immediately halts trading for a strategy, desk, or the firm. SEV-1 / SEV-2 Incident severity levels with defined response and communication requirements. MTTR Mean time to recovery/restore. SLO / SLI / error budget Service Level Objective / Indicator, and the tolerated failure budget. Change failure rate The percentage of production changes that cause an incident or rollback. Lineage The documented path of data from source to use, including transformations. Feature store A system that serves consistent feature definitions to research and production. MLOps Practices and tooling for deploying, monitoring, and governing ML models. P&L attribution Decomposing profit and loss by strategy, desk, instrument, and risk factor. Hurdle rate The minimum return required before profits are shared or capital is allocated.

search.title: Appendix B — Level & title glossary
search.text: High-water mark The peak value that must be recovered before new performance fees/bonuses accrue. Deferral Holding back a portion of variable comp to vest over future years. Clawback Recovering previously paid comp after a restatement, breach, or misconduct. Garden leave Paid notice period during which a departing employee is not permitted to work. Non-compete / non-solicit Contractual restrictions on joining competitors or poaching colleagues; enforceability varies. Carry / LTIP Long-term incentive plan, often tied to firm value or fund profits. Phantom equity A contractual right to a share of value without actual ownership. RFP Request for Proposal; used in vendor and partnership selection. TCA Transaction Cost Analysis; measuring execution quality vs benchmarks. Exchange certification Formal testing required by an exchange before a member can connect or deploy algorithms. Corporate action Events like splits, dividends, mergers, and symbol changes that affect positions and data. Reconciliation break A mismatch between internal records and broker/exchange/custodian records. Settlement / clearing The post-trade process of transferring securities and cash, and the counterparty guarantee in between. Prime broker A bank that provides financing, custody, and settlement services to a trading firm. Counterparty risk The risk that a trading partner, broker, or exchange defaults.

search.title: Appendix B — Level & title glossary
search.text: Liquidity risk The risk of being unable to fund or exit positions at a reasonable price. Surveillance Monitoring for market abuse, manipulation, and policy violations. Best execution The obligation (where applicable) to obtain the best possible result for client orders. MiFID II / EMIR / SEC / CFTC Major regulatory regimes/frameworks; obligations vary by jurisdiction and entity. SR 11-7 US Federal Reserve guidance on model risk management; widely used as a reference standard.

search.title: Appendix C — Promotion packet template
search.text: Appendix C — Promotion packet template Section 1 — Header Section 2 — Scope change (the core test) What will this person own after promotion that they do not own today? Be specific about decisions, horizon, and people. Example: "Owns the short-horizon equity alpha family (4 signals, ~X% of desk risk budget) end-to-end, including the G2/G3 gates, capacity estimates, and the research agenda for one L1 analyst. Currently owns one signal and no research agenda." Section 3 — Evidence (already operating at the next band) Evidence type Specific example Impact (quantified) Date --- --- --- --- Strategy/system delivered Signal X moved to production; net Sharpe Y over 14 months +Z bps of firm P&L; capacity N units Q1–Q4 2026 Scope beyond own work Led the leakage audit standard adopted by 3 pods Reduced failed G2 gates by 40% Q2 2026 Mentorship Mentored 2 L1s; one promoted Both now own modules independently 2025–2026 Cross-functional influence Drove data-quality SLA with CDO team Data incidents down 30% Q3 2026 External signal Presented at [conference]; paper under review Firm brand; recruiting pipeline 2026 Section 4 — Peer and stakeholder feedback Reviewer Relationship Would you trust them at L3?

search.title: Appendix C — Promotion packet template
search.text: (Y/N) Evidence --- --- --- --- [Name] Desk head Y "Owned the strategy through the March drawdown without changing the thesis." [Name] Risk Y "Escalated a limit issue early; proposed a fix." [Name] Peer QR Y "Review comments changed how I test for leakage." Section 5 — Development areas (honest) What is the biggest gap to the next band? (e.g., "has not yet led a cross-team project") What is the plan to close it? (specific, dated) What risk does promotion create? (e.g., "may over-index on research and neglect mentoring") Section 6 — Sponsor statement "I have seen [Name] operate at L3 scope for [period] in [specific situations]. I would trust them to [specific next-band decision] without review. My main reservation is [X], which I believe is manageable because [Y]." Section 7 — Committee decision

search.title: Appendix D — 90-day onboarding plans
search.text: Appendix D — 90-day onboarding plans Universal 30/60/90 structure Phase Goal Deliverables Check-in --- --- --- --- Days 1–30 Learn the firm, the data, the systems, and the people Map of systems and stakeholders; one small shipped fix; 1:1s with 10+ people Week 2 and week 4 with manager Days 31–60 Own a real piece of work with support First independent deliverable; documented assumptions; one design review Week 6 Days 61–90 Operate at band with minimal supervision Owned outcome; written 90-day retrospective; development plan for next 6 months Week 12 Track-specific first 90 days Track Days 1–30 Days 31–60 Days 61–90 --- --- --- --- Research Reproduce a known signal; learn the backtester and cost model; read 5 internal research memos Own a small research question end-to-end; present at research review Deliver a G1/G2-ready memo; identify one dead idea to kill Trading Shadow a trader; learn order types, limits, and kill switches; run a simulated book Run a small live book under supervision; complete an incident drill Own the book within limits; write a strategy note Technology Map the tick-to-trade path; ship a small fix; join on-call shadow Own a module; complete a design review; handle one incident Improve an SLO metric; document a runbook Data/ML Map data sources and lineage; fix one pipeline bug; learn the feature store Own a dataset or pipeline; add tests and monitoring Deliver a data quality improvement with measurable impact Risk Learn every limit and where it is enforced; shadow daily reporting Own a risk domain; run a stress test; challenge one assumption Present a risk finding to the Risk Committee Compliance/Legal Build the obligations register; review filings; meet key exchanges Own a compliance process; draft a policy or contract Complete a mock exam or regulatory review Finance/Treasury Trace a trade from execution to GL; learn the close; meet bankers Own a reconciliation or treasury process Improve close time or funding cost measurably Operations Learn the trade lifecycle; shadow connectivity and settlements Own a process; write a runbook; handle a break Lead an incident drill; automate one manual step Product/Business Interview 10 internal users; map the platform and partners Own a product area or deal pipeline Ship a small improvement or close a deal milestone Onboarding anti-patterns: no named buddy; no first-week deliverable; "read the wiki" as the plan; no introduction to the desks; no clear 90-day success criteria; leaving the new hire to figure out the informal org alone.

search.title: Appendix E — Interview question bank
search.text: Appendix E — Interview question bank Research Walk me through a signal you built. What was the economic mechanism, and how did you test it? How do you detect data leakage in a backtest? Give a specific example. Your signal has a Sharpe of 3 in backtest and 0.5 live. What do you check first? How do you estimate capacity? What changes as capital grows? When would you kill a strategy that is still profitable? Explain a paper you disagree with. Why? How would you test whether a machine-learning model is learning signal vs noise? What is the difference between a statistically significant result and an economically meaningful one? Trading You have a position that is down 2% and your thesis is intact. What do you do? How do you size a position when you are uncertain about your edge? Explain adverse selection in market making. How do you manage it? The market moves against you and your model says stay. How do you decide? What is your worst trade, and what did you learn? How do you know whether your P&L is skill or beta? Walk me through your kill criteria for a strategy. You see an unusual order pattern in the book. What do you do? Technology Design the path from market-data packet to order submission. Where does latency come from? How do you make a lock-free queue correct? What are the memory-ordering pitfalls? You have a p99 latency spike every 5 minutes. How do you debug it?

search.title: Appendix E — Interview question bank
search.text: How do you design a system that must never lose an order? What is your approach to testing a trading system that cannot be tested in production? How do you handle a production incident at 3 a.m. with no obvious cause? When would you choose FPGA over software? What are the trade-offs? How do you prevent a bad deployment from taking down trading? Data / ML Engineering Design a tick-data store for 50 TB with point-in-time queries. What are the trade-offs? How do you make a pipeline idempotent and backfillable? A schema change silently breaks a downstream model. How do you prevent this? How do you detect train/serve skew? How do you govern access to licensed data? What does "data quality" mean for tick data vs reference data? How do you decide between batch and streaming? How do you measure the cost of a data platform? Risk / Model Validation Critique a VaR model that assumes normal returns. What breaks? How would you design limits for a new market-making strategy? A senior trader wants a limit increase during a drawdown. What do you do? How do you validate a machine-learning alpha model? What is the difference between model risk and market risk? How do you stress test a portfolio with options and illiquid positions? What would make you escalate to the board? How do you know your validation is independent enough?

search.title: Appendix E — Interview question bank
search.text: Compliance / Legal A new product launches in two weeks in a new jurisdiction. What do you check? How do you detect spoofing or layering in order data? What are the reporting obligations for the instruments we trade? A trader's personal account trades the same instrument. What is the issue? How do you handle a regulator request for historical order data? When should compliance say "no" vs "here's how"? What data-licensing restrictions apply to alternative data? How do you keep the firm current on regulatory change? Finance / Treasury Trace a trade from execution to the general ledger. Where can it break? How do you build a 13-week cash forecast for a trading firm? What is the cost of holding collateral, and how do you optimize it? How do you attribute P&L to strategy vs market moves? What controls prevent a rogue payment? How do you decide whether to repatriate or reinvest foreign profits? What is the tax risk in a multi-entity trading structure? How do you present risk-adjusted returns to the board? Operations Walk me through the trade lifecycle from order to settlement. An exchange changes its API the day before expiry. What do you do? How do you resolve a reconciliation break that is 3 days old? Design the incident response for a connectivity outage at the open. What is the difference between clearing and settlement? How do you manage corporate actions across 20 venues?

search.title: Appendix E — Interview question bank
search.text: What single-person dependencies exist in your current process? How do you measure operational risk? Product / Business How do you decide what to build for a desk that says "everything is urgent"? Tell me about a product that failed. Why? How do you negotiate an exchange fee schedule? What makes an internal platform adopted vs ignored? How do you measure the ROI of a partnership? A partner misses a deadline that affects trading. What do you do? How do you prioritize between two desks with conflicting needs? What would you stop doing in your first 90 days?

search.title: Appendix G — Further reading
search.text: Appendix G — Further reading Market microstructure and trading Larry Harris, Trading and Exchanges: Market Microstructure for Practitioners — the definitive practitioner reference. Maureen O'Hara, Market Microstructure Theory — the academic foundation. Irene Aldridge, High-Frequency Trading: A Practical Guide to Algorithmic Strategies and Trading Systems — applied HFT. Robert Carver, Systematic Trading and Leveraged Trading — portfolio construction and realistic backtesting for systematic traders. Ernest Chan, Algorithmic Trading: Winning Strategies and Their Rationale — accessible strategy design with code. Research methodology and overfitting Marcos López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning — data structures, labeling, backtest pitfalls. Marcos López de Prado, Machine Learning for Asset Managers — compact treatment of ML in portfolio construction. Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado, Zhu, "The Probability of Backtest Overfitting" — the deflated Sharpe framework. Bailey & López de Prado, "The Deflated Sharpe Ratio" — correcting for selection bias. Grinold & Kahn, Active Portfolio Management — the canonical text on alpha, risk, and portfolio construction. David Aronson, Evidence-Based Technical Analysis — statistical rigor for trading rules. Risk and governance John Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions — comprehensive risk framework.

search.title: Appendix G — Further reading
search.text: Philippe Jorion, Value at Risk — VaR/ES foundations and limitations. Federal Reserve SR 11-7, Guidance on Model Risk Management — the reference standard for model risk. Basel Committee papers on stress testing and risk appetite — framework language regulators expect. Nassim Taleb, Antifragile and The Black Swan — tail-risk intuition (read critically). Engineering and reliability Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — data systems foundations. Google SRE team, Site Reliability Engineering and The Site Reliability Workbook — SLOs, error budgets, incident management. Will Larson, Staff Engineer — the IC leadership path. Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle — engineering org design and management. Camille Fournier, The Manager's Path — the transition from IC to manager. Andy Grove, High Output Management — the classic on managerial leverage. Firm strategy and history Gregory Zuckerman, The Man Who Solved the Market — Renaissance Technologies and the culture of quant research. Sebastian Mallaby, More Money Than God — hedge fund history and strategy evolution. Scott Patterson, Dark Pools — the rise of electronic trading and HFT. Michael Lewis, Flash Boys — readable but polemical; read alongside Harris and Patterson. Execution and market making theory Almgren & Chriss, "Optimal Execution of Portfolio Transactions" — the foundational execution model.

search.title: Appendix G — Further reading
search.text: Avellaneda & Stoikov, "High-Frequency Trading in a Limit Order Book" — market-making model. Robert Almgren, "Execution Risk" — practical treatment of execution uncertainty. Regulatory references (jurisdiction-specific; verify current versions) SEC Rule 15c3-5 (Market Access Rule) — pre-trade risk controls for US broker-dealers. MiFID II / MiFIR, including RTS 6 on algorithmic trading — EU algorithmic controls and reporting. EMIR — EU derivatives clearing and reporting. CFTC Part 43/45 — US swaps reporting (where applicable). Local exchange rulebooks — connectivity, certification, and market-conduct rules. Companion resource in this workspace youtube-quant-hft-resources.md — a curated list of ~95 quant/HFT talks, lectures, and channels for ongoing learning.

search.title: Appendix H — Original source text (preserved verbatim)
search.text: Appendix H — Original source text (preserved verbatim) This appendix reproduces the two sections supplied at the start of the project, exactly as written, so the source of the framework is never lost. Part II expands Section 1; Part III (§11–§14) and Part IV expand Section 2.

search.title: Appendix H — Original source text (preserved verbatim)
search.heading: H.1 Core Domains & Job Titles
search.text: Research & Strategy Quantitative Researcher (QR) / Alpha Researcher: Builds statistical, econometric, and machine learning models to predict short-term price moves and market microstructure signals. Execution / Microstructure Researcher: Studies order-book dynamics, queue position, slippage, and optimal order routing. Data Quant / Alternative Data Researcher: Sources, cleans, and models tick data, order books, news, and alternative datasets. Trading & Portfolio Management Quantitative Trader (QT): Runs live strategies, monitors risk and P&L, tunes parameters, and manages intraday/short-horizon exposures. Execution Trader: Focuses on low-impact order execution, liquidity provision, and market making across exchanges. Portfolio Manager (PM) / Quant PM: Owns P&L for a book or strategy pod, allocates capital and risk limits, and leads researchers/traders. Software, Low-Latency & Hardware Engineering Quantitative Developer (QD): Turns research models and trading logic into fast, reliable production code (heavily C++, Rust, or Python). Low-Latency / HFT Systems Engineer: Optimizes kernel bypass, networking, lock-free concurrency, and tick-to-trade latency. FPGA / Hardware Engineer: Designs custom hardware logic (Verilog/VHDL/FPGA) for ultra-low-latency market data decoding and order execution.

search.title: Appendix H — Original source text (preserved verbatim)
search.heading: H.1 Core Domains & Job Titles
search.text: Core / Infrastructure / SRE / DevOps Engineer: Builds distributed compute clusters, simulation/backtesting pipelines, telemetry, and production reliability. Data, Risk & Control Data Engineer / Machine Learning Engineer: Builds petabyte-scale historical tick storage, feature pipelines, and ML training infrastructure. Quantitative Risk Manager / Risk Engineer: Monitors real-time exposure, stress tests tail risk, enforces margin/position limits, and validates models. Model Validation Quant: Independently tests pricing, risk, and statistical assumptions for accuracy and robustness. Operations & Corporate Functions Trading Operations / Market Ops: Handles exchange connectivity, corporate actions, reconciliations, and live incident response. Compliance, Legal & Finance: Manages regulatory reporting, exchange rules, treasury, and firm accounting.

search.title: Appendix H — Original source text (preserved verbatim)
search.heading: H.2 Typical Ranks & Career Progression
search.text: Exact titles vary by firm, but most HFT and quant shops follow a flat-to-tiered meritocratic ladder tied closely to P&L or technical impact: Intern / Summer Analyst: Short-term research, trading simulation, or coding projects; primary pipeline for full-time offers. Junior / Associate / Analyst (Entry-Level, ~0–2 yrs): Executes defined research tasks, builds basic tools, or assists on live trading desks under supervision. Mid-Level Quant / Trader / Developer (~2–5 yrs): Independently owns signals, trading books, or core low-latency systems. Senior Quant / Senior Trader / Senior Engineer (~5+ yrs): Leads complex strategies or mission-critical infrastructure and mentors junior staff. Vice President (VP) / Director / Principal: Used more often at banks and larger multi-strat funds; denotes high technical or desk authority. Portfolio Manager (PM) / Head of Desk: Runs a standalone profit center or team with explicit capital and risk budgets. Managing Director (MD) / Partner / C-Suite (CEO, CTO, CRO, Head of Quant): Shapes firm-wide strategy, capital allocation, risk governance, and leadership. Mapping to this document: H.1 is expanded in Part II (with scope notes, interfaces, and bands); H.2 is preserved and mapped to the unified ladder in §11 ("The original seven-rank ladder") and expanded into full journeys in Part IV.

search.title: Closing note
search.text: Closing note This framework is a default, not a dogma. The bands, gates, and committees exist to make the implicit explicit — so that a firm can grow without losing the things that made it good: small teams, fast decisions, real ownership, and an honest relationship with risk. Three questions to ask every year: Is our structure still following our edge? If the edge moved, the org should move. Do our levels still mean something? If a band no longer predicts scope, fix the calibration. Would a strong person join us and know how to grow here? If not, the career framework is not finished. Version 1.0 · November 2026 · Maintained by the CEO office. Review annually, or whenever the firm crosses a scaling threshold.
